title: Accountants and auditors
rationale: Core accounting and auditing work — examining financial records, computing taxes, analyzing data, identifying risks, preparing reports — is overwhelmingly digital and cognitive, putting it directly in AI's path; routine tasks like data entry, reconciliation, and document review are already being automated by AI and RPA tools. Demand elasticity is moderate because cheaper, faster financial analysis unlocks some latent demand (more small businesses get proper advisory services, more granular analysis, more frequent auditing), but core demand is structurally capped by regulatory requirements, the fixed number of entities needing audits, and the fact that compliance needs don't multiply with lower cost. The combination of very high disruption with moderate elasticity means the occupation persists but shifts decisively toward advisory, judgment, and client-facing roles while routine preparation work shrinks, requiring workers to substantially upskill — the hallmark of restructuring rather than wholesale replacement.

title: Actors
rationale: Acting's core involves physical, embodied performance and the human appeal of recognizable performers, which AI cannot fully replicate, but AI is encroaching on voiceover, background/extra work, digital doubles, and synthetic media — pushing disruption to a moderate level. Demand for content is somewhat elastic as cheaper production unlocks more video and media, but the value of human celebrity and live performance caps how much AI productivity translates into more human acting work. Because the disruption score sits at or below 6 and the human-presence core remains intact, the occupation is best categorized as resilient, with AI eroding certain subfields (extras, voiceover) rather than reshaping the central craft.

title: Actuaries
rationale: Actuarial work is predominantly digital and cognitive—statistical modeling, data analysis, forecasting, and report generation—which are squarely in AI's path, driving a high disruption score. However, demand elasticity is low because the volume of insurance products, regulatory filings, and risk assessments is structurally and regulatorily constrained; cheaper actuarial output does not unlock dramatically more demand, and certification requirements gate the role rather than expand its scope. While BLS projects strong nominal growth, AI productivity gains are likely to compress per-task headcount needs, so the combination of high disruption and limited demand expansion fits the replace category, though strong projected growth and the heavy communication/judgment component may soften the contraction toward restructuring.

title: Administrative services and facilities managers
rationale: The role mixes significant knowledge work (records management, procurement analysis, scheduling, compliance documentation) that AI can streamline with substantial physical-presence and human-coordination duties — supervising maintenance staff, monitoring buildings, handling on-call emergencies, and managing renovation projects. AI will automate the administrative and recordkeeping portions but cannot replace the oversight of physical facilities and people management, capping disruption at moderate. Demand is structurally tied to the number of buildings and organizations needing management rather than to cost suppression, so productivity gains mostly reduce per-manager workload rather than unlocking large latent demand, yielding low elasticity. Because disruption stays at or below 6, the occupation is resilient — AI reshapes peripheral tasks but not the core supervisory and facilities-oversight work.

title: Adult basic and secondary education and ESL teachers
rationale: The core work involves in-person instruction, motivating adult learners, cultural sensitivity, and adapting to diverse abilities — tasks requiring human presence and interpersonal judgment that AI cannot fully replace, though AI tutoring tools materially assist lesson planning, language practice, and individualized instruction, placing disruption at the moderate-to-high boundary. Demand has some latent elasticity since cheaper personalized language and literacy instruction could expand access, but structural factors like declining enrollment, government funding constraints, and the social/motivational nature of these classroom programs cap that growth at moderate. Because the disruption score lands at 6 — AI augments planning and practice but does not reshape the human-centered core of teaching adult learners — this occupation fits the resilient category rather than restructure.

title: Advertising sales agents
rationale: The work is predominantly digital and language-based — prospecting, drafting proposals, preparing reports, analyzing sales statistics, and ad placement — much of which is already being automated by programmatic ad-buying platforms and AI-assisted CRM/outreach tools, driving high disruption. Demand elasticity is low: advertising budgets are constrained by client revenue and marketing spend, and the shift to automated programmatic ad placement directly removes the human intermediary rather than expanding the need for agents, as reflected in the BLS -6% projection. Productivity gains accrue to platforms and tools rather than unlocking dramatically more human-sold ad inventory. With disruption at 7 and elasticity at 4, headcount contraction is the expected outcome, fitting the replace category.

title: Advertising, promotions, and marketing managers
rationale: Marketing management is predominantly knowledge work—campaign planning, content strategy, market analysis, copy generation, ad placement, and audience segmentation are all directly in AI's path, with generative AI and automated ad platforms already materially changing daily workflows. However, marketing demand is highly elastic: cheaper and faster content production, personalization, and analytics unlock vastly more campaigns, channels, micro-segments, and continuous optimization that were previously cost-prohibitive. Because productivity gains expand the total volume of marketing output rather than simply reducing headcount, demand absorbs the disruption, and the managerial layer (strategy, judgment, client relationships, brand stewardship) remains essential to direct AI tools. This fits 'augment'—each manager produces far more output while overall employment stays stable or grows.

title: Aerospace engineering and operations technologists and technicians
rationale: The core work involves substantial physical, hands-on tasks—building and maintaining test facilities, installing parts and instruments in aircraft, calibrating wind tunnels, and assembly—that require real-world presence and cannot be automated by AI. AI does meaningfully assist the digital portions (running computer simulations, recording and analyzing test data, programming test equipment), pushing disruption to a moderate level, but the manual and on-site safety-critical work anchors the role. Demand elasticity is moderate-to-high because cheaper satellite launches, drones, and new aircraft types are expanding the aerospace sector, suggesting productivity gains would be absorbed by more testing and production rather than headcount cuts. With disruption at or below 6, the occupation is best classified as resilient—AI augments the analytical periphery but the physical core endures.

title: Aerospace engineers
rationale: Aerospace engineering is predominantly knowledge work centered on design, simulation, analysis, and computational modeling — all directly in AI's path, with generative design, automated CFD/FEA optimization, and AI-assisted testing already reshaping workflows, driving a high disruption score. However, the work also requires physical prototyping, regulatory compliance, security-cleared defense work, and team coordination that anchor a human role. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper, faster design unlocks meaningful latent demand in expanding markets like small satellites, drones, and commercial space, but growth is capped by capital intensity, safety regulation, and the limited number of major aerospace programs. Disruption >=7 with elasticity of 6 places this in restructure — the occupation persists and grows modestly, but skill sets shift toward AI-augmented design and systems integration, displacing engineers who don't adapt.

title: Agricultural and food science technicians
rationale: The work mixes physical hands-on tasks—collecting and preparing samples, operating lab and farm equipment, inspecting food in processing plants—with cognitive tasks like analyzing test results and preparing reports. AI can assist with the data analysis and reporting portions, but the core requires physical presence in labs, farms, and processing plants for sample collection, equipment operation, and inspection, which keeps disruption moderate. Demand could expand modestly as cheaper analysis enables more agricultural research and quality control, but it is structurally tied to regulatory testing requirements and physical throughput rather than unlimited latent demand. Since disruption stays at or below 6, the occupation is resilient: AI augments the analytical periphery but does not reshape the fundamentally physical, presence-dependent core work.

title: Agricultural and food scientists
rationale: The work mixes substantial cognitive components (data analysis, experiment design, literature review, modeling crop/animal genetics) where AI is already materially useful, with significant physical and field-based requirements (lab experiments, farm visits, sample collection, biosecurity compliance) that AI cannot perform. This blend places disruption at moderate (5) — AI accelerates analysis and hypothesis generation but cannot replace the hands-on empirical core. Elasticity is moderate (6) because cheaper, faster research could unlock more agricultural innovation given pressing demands around climate, pests, water resources, and food safety, though regulatory validation and physical experimentation cap expansion. Because disruption is at or below 6, the occupation is classified resilient: AI reshapes the analytical periphery but the empirical, field-bound core work remains intact.

title: Agricultural engineers
rationale: A meaningful portion of the work is digital and cognitive—CAD design, systems modeling, data analysis, and integrating AI/geospatial systems—which AI tools materially accelerate, but the core role still requires substantial physical presence at farms, labs, and construction sites, plus hands-on oversight of equipment and facilities, capping disruption at moderate. Elasticity is moderate because cheaper, faster engineering could unlock more precision-agriculture and automation projects as farmers seek cost reductions, but the field is small and constrained by capital-intensive agricultural cycles and slow adoption. Since disruption is 6 (below the 7 threshold) and the physical, multi-stakeholder nature of the work limits full automation, the occupation is best classified as resilient—AI reshapes the design and analysis periphery but does not displace the integrated engineering role.

title: Agricultural workers
rationale: Core tasks are overwhelmingly physical—planting, harvesting, herding, feeding livestock, operating machinery in unpredictable outdoor conditions—which AI software cannot perform directly. Disruption comes mainly from physical automation (robotic harvesters, automated tractors) rather than AI cognitive tools, and these mechanization gains shift work toward equipment operators rather than eliminating the occupation through AI. Demand for agricultural output is relatively inelastic since food consumption is fairly fixed and productivity gains historically reduce labor headcount rather than expand it. With disruption well below 6, this occupation is resilient to AI in the language/cognitive sense, even though it faces slow employment decline from physical mechanization.

title: Air traffic controllers
rationale: Air traffic control is heavily cognitive and data-driven, and AI/automation systems like NextGen already increase per-controller capacity, suggesting meaningful disruption to workflow. However, the core work involves real-time, life-safety decision-making under strict regulatory accountability where full automation is socially and legally constrained, keeping humans firmly in the loop and capping disruption at moderate. Demand is highly inelastic — the number of flights to coordinate is fixed by air traffic volume, not by the cost or speed of control services, so productivity gains translate into modestly more traffic handled per controller rather than expanded demand. Because disruption stays at or below 6 and the role's safety-critical human-in-the-loop nature is durable, this occupation is resilient.

title: Aircraft and avionics equipment mechanics and technicians
rationale: The core work is hands-on physical repair, inspection, and maintenance of aircraft requiring dexterity, physical strength, and in-person presence in hangars and on airfields — tasks largely outside AI's direct reach. AI may assist with diagnostics, predictive maintenance scheduling, and interpreting test data, but these are peripheral aids that don't replace the manual labor or FAA-regulated certification requirements. Demand is structurally tied to fleet size and flight hours and is heavily constrained by safety regulation, so productivity gains wouldn't dramatically expand the volume of physical maintenance needed. With disruption well below 6, the occupation is resilient: AI touches the periphery while the regulated, physical core remains intact.

title: Airline and commercial pilots
rationale: While modern aircraft are heavily automated and AI can enhance flight planning, autopilot, and systems monitoring, the core work of piloting requires physical presence in the cockpit, real-time judgment in emergencies, and—critically—deep regulatory and safety/liability constraints that mandate certified human pilots for the next decade and beyond. Passenger trust and FAA certification requirements make full autonomy implausible within 10 years, so AI touches only the periphery (planning, monitoring, copilot assistance). Demand for air travel is moderately elastic—cheaper operations could expand routes and frequency—but pilot headcount per flight is regulated and unlikely to compress significantly. With disruption well below the threshold, this occupation is resilient: AI augments tools but does not reshape the fundamental human-in-the-loop nature of flying.

title: Animal care and service workers
rationale: The core work — feeding, grooming, bathing, exercising, and physically handling unpredictable live animals — is almost entirely hands-on physical labor requiring real-world presence, compassion, and tactile skill that AI cannot perform. AI touches only peripheral tasks like scheduling, record-keeping, and behavior monitoring. Demand is moderately elastic, growing with pet ownership and willingness to spend, but it is constrained by the physical nature of the service rather than cost or speed of cognition. With disruption far below the threshold, this occupation is clearly resilient.

title: Announcers and DJs
rationale: The occupation is split: broadcast announcers and radio DJs do predominantly digital/voice-based work that AI voice synthesis can already replicate, and stations are explicitly adopting AI DJs, but party DJs and emcees (40% of the field) require physical presence at live events that AI cannot replace. This dual nature pulls the disruption score to moderate rather than high. Elasticity is low because demand for radio airtime and live event hosting is structurally capped—cheaper AI announcing does not meaningfully expand the number of weddings, clubs, or radio slots needing a host. Because disruption sits at 6, with the live-event segment insulated and even growing, the occupation overall is resilient even as the broadcast subsegment contracts.

title: Anthropologists and archeologists
rationale: The work mixes significant digital/cognitive components (data analysis, report writing, literature synthesis, GIS, linguistic and pattern analysis) that AI materially assists with, but core tasks require fieldwork, physical excavation, in-person observation, interviews, and on-site regulatory compliance assessment that AI cannot perform. Demand is largely fixed by research funding, federal preservation regulations, and limited corporate market-research budgets, so cheaper analysis would not dramatically expand the number of excavations or studies undertaken. Because disruption is only moderate (5) — AI touches the analytical periphery but not the irreducible field-based core — the occupation is resilient, with stable modest growth driven by regulatory needs rather than productivity-driven contraction.

title: Arbitrators, mediators, and conciliators
rationale: The work involves document analysis, applying rules and precedent, and preparing settlement agreements—all knowledge-based tasks AI can assist with—but the core function is facilitating trust, emotionally charged human negotiation, and rendering legitimate, often legally binding decisions that require neutral human authority and presence. Parties want a credible human third party for emotionally fraught disputes, so AI mostly augments preparation and analysis rather than replacing the central role. Demand is somewhat constrained by the structural reality that arbitration/mediation volume is tied to existing disputes, regulatory mandates, and government budgets rather than being heavily price-suppressed. Because disruption stays at or below 6, the occupation is resilient: AI touches the analytical periphery but does not reshape the fundamentally interpersonal and authority-based core work.

title: Architects
rationale: Much of an architect's work — design iteration, CADD/BIM modeling, drawing production, code research, cost estimation, and specifications — is digital and cognitive, putting it squarely in AI's path; generative design and AI-assisted BIM already materially change workflows, driving a high disruption score. Demand is moderately elastic: cheaper, faster design could unlock more renovation, custom, and small-project work, but construction demand is ultimately gated by capital costs, permitting, regulation, and the physical building cycle, capping expansion. Because disruption is high (7) and elasticity is moderate (6), the occupation survives but shifts: routine drafting and documentation get automated while architects move toward client management, conceptual design, site oversight, and broader project roles — workers who master AI tools thrive, those who don't are displaced.

title: Architectural and engineering managers
rationale: The core work blends knowledge tasks AI can assist (technical analysis, planning, budgeting, design review, documentation) with substantial human-centric responsibilities — leadership, hiring, motivating teams, accountability for projects, stakeholder coordination, and on-site oversight of construction or manufacturing. AI materially augments the analytical and documentation portions but cannot assume managerial judgment, organizational responsibility, or interpersonal leadership, capping disruption at moderate. Elasticity is moderate because cheaper engineering and design output (driven by infrastructure repair, grid expansion, and renewable energy projects) could unlock more projects requiring managerial oversight, but management headcount scales sublinearly with output and is constrained by organizational structure. Since disruption is at or below 6, the occupation is best classified as resilient — AI reshapes the technical periphery without displacing the leadership core.

title: Archivists, curators, and museum workers
rationale: The work is split: archivists' cataloging, digitization, metadata management, and electronic-records organization are squarely in AI's path, while curators' physical handling, conservation restoration, exhibit preparation, and public-facing duties require human presence and hands-on craft. AI materially assists the digital/knowledge portions (classification, transcription, search, condition documentation) but cannot perform the physical preservation, authentication touch, and institutional/civic functions, keeping disruption moderate. Demand is structurally constrained by museum and government budgets and public interest rather than cost-of-output, so productivity gains free up staff for backlog work but don't unlock dramatic new demand. Since disruption stays at or below 6, the occupation is resilient—AI reshapes peripheral and digital tasks without overturning the core.

title: Art directors
rationale: Art direction is predominantly digital, conceptual, and visual work — much of it (mood boards, layout drafts, image generation, design iteration) is directly in the path of generative AI tools that already materially change creative workflows, driving a high disruption score. However, the core role blends client communication, creative vision, leadership, and final judgment that AI augments rather than replaces. Demand for visual content is highly elastic: as production becomes cheaper and faster, businesses, media, and individuals consume far more visual output across web, video, advertising, and packaging, unlocking latent demand. With disruption >=7 and elasticity >=7, art directors fit augment — each director orchestrates AI-assisted output to produce dramatically more, keeping headcount stable to growing.

title: Assemblers and fabricators
rationale: Core work is physical and manual—positioning, aligning, fastening, soldering, welding parts requiring dexterity, hand-eye coordination, and physical strength—which AI software cannot perform directly; disruption comes from physical robotics and automation rather than AI per se, so the AI-specific disruption score is low. Demand is largely fixed by physical product output and capped by offshoring dynamics and capital investment, so productivity gains from automation translate to fewer workers rather than expanded headcount, as reflected in the projected employment decline. While some segments (EV batteries, semiconductors) grow, the occupation overall is constrained. Because disruption to the core hands-on work from AI specifically is low, the occupation is best classified as resilient even though automation pressures gradually erode headcount.

title: Athletes and sports competitors
rationale: The core work of professional athletes is inherently physical, requiring human athleticism, hand-eye coordination, stamina, and real-time competition that AI cannot perform or replace. AI touches only peripheral activities like performance analysis, opponent scouting, and injury prevention, leaving the actual competing entirely human. Demand is highly constrained by the fixed number of league roster spots and the rarity of franchise expansion, so even cheaper training tools would not expand headcount substantially. With disruption far below the threshold, this occupation is clearly resilient to AI.

title: Athletic trainers
rationale: Athletic training is overwhelmingly hands-on physical work — applying tape and braces, providing on-field emergency care, manual rehabilitation, and real-time injury evaluation requiring physical presence. AI touches only peripheral tasks like record-keeping, report writing, and possibly diagnostic support, leaving the physical core untouched. Demand is moderately elastic given growing sports participation and aging active adults, but the work itself is not gated by cost of cognitive tasks. With disruption well below 7, this occupation is resilient: AI augments documentation but does not reshape the core hands-on work.

title: Atmospheric scientists, including meteorologists
rationale: The work is predominantly computational and data-driven—running atmospheric models, analyzing satellite/radar data, writing programs, and generating forecasts—all squarely in AI's path, with ML-based weather prediction already outperforming traditional numerical models in some benchmarks. Demand has moderate elasticity: cheaper, faster, more accurate forecasting unlocks latent demand for specialized commercial forecasting (logistics, energy, agriculture, just-in-time delivery) and more granular hyperlocal products, but core public/government roles are funding-constrained and the total market is relatively small and fixed. The forecasting and modeling core can be heavily automated while human roles shift toward model oversight, interpretation, severe-weather decision-making, client-specific analysis, broadcast communication, and forensic/research work. This combination of high disruption and moderate elasticity fits restructure—the occupation persists but skills shift toward AI-augmented analysis and judgment rather than manual modeling.

title: Audiologists
rationale: Audiology combines diagnostic interpretation (where AI can assist with analyzing audiometry results and tuning hearing aids) with hands-on physical care like ear cleaning, device fitting, cochlear implant collaboration, and balance exercises that require in-person presence. The disruption score is moderate because AI augments the testing and diagnostic analysis but the core treatment, counseling, and physical examination remain human-centered and require licensure. Demand is moderately elastic given an aging population, growing infant screening, and underdiagnosed hearing loss—cheaper, faster diagnostics could unlock latent demand. Since disruption is at or below 6, this occupation is resilient: AI touches diagnostic periphery but does not reshape the hands-on, patient-facing core.

title: Automotive body and glass repairers
rationale: The core work—hammering out dents, welding parts, removing and installing glass, aligning frames—is physically demanding, hands-on, and requires real-world presence and dexterity that AI cannot replace. AI touches only peripheral tasks like damage estimation and diagnostic calibration of sensors/cameras, leaving the manual repair work essentially unchanged. Demand is structurally inelastic since it depends on collision frequency, which is actually declining due to vehicle safety features, so productivity gains cannot meaningfully expand the market. With disruption well below 6, this occupation is clearly resilient regardless of elasticity.

title: Automotive service technicians and mechanics
rationale: The core work is overwhelmingly physical—lifting parts, working in awkward positions, disassembling and reassembling components—which AI cannot perform; AI improves only the diagnostic portion via better computerized scan tools and fault prediction. While modern vehicles are increasingly electronic, the hands-on repair remains irreplaceable in the near term, keeping disruption low. Demand is tied to the physical vehicle fleet and is relatively inelastic—cheaper diagnostics won't make people repair their cars dramatically more often, and EVs may actually reduce maintenance needs. With disruption well below 6, this occupation is resilient: AI augments diagnosis at the periphery but does not reshape the fundamentally manual nature of the job.

title: Bakers
rationale: Baking is overwhelmingly physical and hands-on work — measuring, kneading, shaping dough, monitoring ovens, decorating, and cleaning — that requires real-world presence and manual dexterity that AI cannot perform; AI only touches peripheral tasks like recipe scaling, inventory, or scheduling. Demand for baked goods is relatively stable and tied to food consumption, which is constrained by appetite and population rather than cost or speed of production, so productivity gains would not unleash explosive new demand. With disruption well below the threshold, the occupation is resilient: AI affects only the administrative edges while the core craft remains human-dependent.

title: Barbers, hairstylists, and cosmetologists
rationale: The core work is entirely physical and hands-on—cutting, coloring, and styling hair require manual dexterity, in-person presence, and tactile judgment that AI cannot perform. AI is irrelevant to the actual service and touches only peripheral tasks like appointment scheduling or inventory management. Demand is largely fixed by biological hair growth and personal grooming habits, so even if AI made back-office tasks cheaper, people don't need dramatically more haircuts. With disruption far below the threshold, this occupation is clearly resilient.

title: Bartenders
rationale: Bartending is overwhelmingly physical and interpersonal — mixing drinks, serving, monitoring intoxication, checking IDs, and engaging customers all require human presence and dexterity, so AI touches only peripheral functions like inventory management or POS systems. The core social and hospitality experience that draws people to bars cannot be automated meaningfully. Demand is somewhat tied to discretionary income and the social atmosphere customers seek, which limits how much cheaper service would expand consumption. With disruption well below 7, the occupation is clearly resilient: AI may streamline ordering or stocking, but the hands-on, face-to-face nature of the work remains intact.

title: Bill and account collectors
rationale: The work is almost entirely digital and language-based — phone negotiations, skip tracing via databases, record updating, and applying scripted legal disclosures — all squarely in the path of AI voice agents, automated dialers, and NLP-driven negotiation tools. Demand is highly inelastic: the volume of overdue debt is fixed by the economy and lending activity, not suppressed by collection cost, so making collection cheaper simply lets fewer workers handle the same accounts rather than expanding total work. The BLS already projects a 10% decline driven by automation. High disruption combined with low elasticity yields clear headcount contraction, fitting the replace category.

title: Biochemists and biophysicists
rationale: Much of the analytical, computational modeling, literature review, data mining, and report-writing work is directly in AI's path, and AI tools like protein-structure prediction (e.g., AlphaFold) already materially transform parts of this field. However, the core requires substantial hands-on wet-lab experimentation, physical manipulation of biological samples, and team-based research presence that AI cannot replace, keeping disruption moderate at 6. Demand elasticity is high because cheaper and faster discovery accelerates drug development, diagnostics, and biotech research where latent demand is enormous and currently bottlenecked by cost and time. Because disruption is at or below 6, the occupation is classified as resilient — AI dramatically augments the knowledge-work portions but does not reshape the physically grounded experimental core.

title: Bioengineers and biomedical engineers
rationale: Much of the design, simulation, statistical modeling, and technical reporting work is digital and directly aided by AI, but core tasks like installing/maintaining biomedical equipment, hands-on device testing in hospitals, clinician training, and physical prototyping require real-world presence, keeping disruption moderate at 6. Demand is genuinely elastic — cheaper and faster R&D would unlock more medical devices, drug therapies, and personalized solutions, since healthcare needs vastly exceed current supply. Because disruption is at or below 6, the occupation lands in 'resilient': AI substantially augments the knowledge-work portions but does not reshape the physical, regulated, and collaborative core of the work.

title: Biological technicians
rationale: The work blends significant physical lab tasks (setting up equipment, preparing biological samples, conducting bench experiments, fieldwork) with cognitive tasks (data analysis, reporting) that AI can accelerate. AI tools can materially assist the documentation, data interpretation, and modeling portions, but the hands-on wet-lab work requires physical presence and cannot be automated by current AI, capping disruption at moderate. Demand has moderate elasticity since cheaper, faster research could expand biotech and synthetic biology projects, but growth is constrained by funding, regulatory, and physical-lab capacity limits. Because disruption stays at or below 6, the occupation is resilient — AI augments the analytical periphery while the core physical and observational lab work remains human-dependent.

title: Boilermakers
rationale: Boilermaking is overwhelmingly physical and hands-on work performed in cramped, dangerous, real-world environments—welding, riveting, aligning heavy plates, inspecting confined spaces—none of which AI can perform; only peripheral tasks like blueprint reading have any digital component, yielding a very low disruption score. Demand is structurally constrained by the slow installation/maintenance cycle of long-lived boilers and the secular shift away from coal-fired generation, so even dramatically cheaper analysis would not expand headcount needs. Because disruption is far below the threshold for any AI-driven category, this occupation is resilient; its modest projected decline stems from energy-market trends rather than automation.

title: Bookkeeping, accounting, and auditing clerks
rationale: The core work—data entry, posting transactions, reconciling accounts, checking figures, and producing financial reports—is almost entirely digital, rule-based, and routine, placing it directly in AI's path; accounting software and AI already automate most of these tasks, justifying a very high disruption score. Demand for bookkeeping is structurally fixed: a business needs its books reconciled once, and making this cheaper or faster does not cause organizations to demand dramatically more bookkeeping, so productivity gains convert directly into fewer workers rather than more output. With disruption of 9 and elasticity of 2, this is a clear replace case, consistent with the BLS projection of declining employment as automation lets the same work be done with fewer clerks.

title: Broadcast, sound, and video technicians
rationale: Disruption is moderate: the editing, mixing, and signal-processing portions of this work are increasingly automated by AI tools (auto-mixing, AI audio cleanup, automated camera switching), but the core work involves physically setting up, rigging, dismantling, and operating equipment on location, climbing towers, hauling gear, and troubleshooting hardware in real time—all requiring human presence. Elasticity is moderate because cheaper, faster production unlocks more content and live events (digital signage, video conferencing, podcasts, streaming) expanding demand in some segments, while broadcast and traditional studio roles contract. Because the disruption score is at or below 6 and the physical, on-site nature of the work shields the core tasks, the occupation is best classified as resilient—AI reshapes the digital editing periphery and lets fewer technicians do more, but does not eliminate the hands-on core.

title: Budget analysts
rationale: Budget analysis is almost entirely digital, cognitive, and language-based work—data analysis, cost-benefit modeling, report writing, and spending monitoring all sit directly in AI's path, and current AI tools already automate much of the data processing and report generation. Demand is structurally fixed because budgets correspond to a fixed number of organizations and government entities with set fiscal cycles; making analysis cheaper doesn't cause organizations to produce 10x more budgets. With high disruption and inelastic demand, productivity gains translate into fewer analysts per organization rather than expanded output, supporting the replace category, consistent with the BLS-projected near-flat 1% growth.

title: Bus drivers
rationale: Bus driving is overwhelmingly physical and presence-based: operating a vehicle in unpredictable real-world conditions, managing passenger safety, assisting riders with disabilities, and handling unruly passengers. While autonomous vehicle technology is advancing, regulatory barriers, the unstructured nature of passenger transit (especially school buses with children and supervisory duties), and safety liability mean full self-driving buses are not near deployment at scale within 10 years. Demand is structurally constrained by fixed routes, school enrollment trends, and public transit budgets, so even cheaper operation would not dramatically expand ridership. The low disruption score places this firmly in the resilient category regardless of elasticity.

title: Butchers
rationale: Butchering is almost entirely physical and manual—cutting, deboning, trimming, lifting heavy carcasses, and handling sharp tools in cold rooms—tasks requiring fine motor dexterity and real-world presence that AI cannot perform without advanced robotics that remain immature and expensive. AI could only touch peripheral admin tasks like inventory tracking or demand forecasting, leaving the core work untouched. Demand for fresh meat cutting is fixed by food consumption patterns and would not expand dramatically even if cheaper. With disruption far below the threshold, this occupation is clearly resilient to AI over the next decade.

title: Calibration technologists and technicians
rationale: The core work involves physically inspecting, adjusting, and testing measurement devices with hands-on dexterity, lifting equipment, and working in plants and labs — tasks that require human presence and manual manipulation. AI and self-calibrating devices can automate some routine readings and documentation, but the physical and judgment-based core remains, placing disruption at the moderate-low end. Demand could expand modestly as automation increases measurement device complexity and more equipment requires calibration, but the niche, regulation-bound nature of metrology caps explosive growth. Because disruption stays at or below 6, the occupation is resilient: AI touches peripheral admin and self-calibration features but does not reshape the hands-on metrology work.

title: Cardiovascular technologists and technicians
rationale: The core work involves hands-on patient preparation, positioning, operating physical equipment, assisting in invasive procedures, and lifting patients—tasks requiring physical presence that AI cannot perform. AI meaningfully assists the cognitive portions (analyzing test results, flagging abnormalities, EKG interpretation), but these are a minority of daily duties, keeping disruption moderate. Demand is somewhat elastic given an aging population and rising cardiovascular disease prevalence, but capacity is constrained by physical procedure volumes and clinical settings. Because disruption is at or below 6, the occupation is resilient: AI augments diagnostic interpretation but does not reshape the fundamentally physical, patient-facing core of the role.

title: Career and technical education teachers
rationale: CTE teaching is fundamentally hands-on and physical—demonstrating welding, brake repair, cosmetology, or culinary techniques requires in-person supervision, safety oversight, and tactile skill transfer that AI cannot replace. AI will assist with peripheral tasks like lesson planning, generating assessments, and supplementing instruction, but the core of demonstrating and supervising hands-on skill development requires human presence in workshops and labs. Demand elasticity is moderate since cheaper instruction could expand vocational training access, but enrollment is structurally constrained by declining student populations, fixed budgets, and government funding limits. With disruption at 4, the occupation is resilient: AI touches the administrative periphery but does not reshape the experiential, physical core of teaching trades.

title: Carpenters
rationale: Carpentry is overwhelmingly physical, hands-on work requiring dexterity, on-site presence, and real-time problem-solving in variable, unpredictable environments—core tasks AI cannot perform. AI touches only peripheral aspects like blueprint reading, planning, and material calculations, while prefabrication (a manufacturing trend, not AI) poses a larger structural threat. Demand could expand moderately if construction costs drop, since housing demand is partly cost-suppressed, but physical labor caps productivity gains. With disruption far below 7, this occupation is clearly resilient to AI.

title: Cartographers and photogrammetrists
rationale: The work is predominantly digital and cognitive—collecting, analyzing, and visualizing geospatial data using GIS, CAD, and remote sensing software—all of which are directly in AI's path; automated feature extraction, LiDAR processing, and map generation already materially change the workflow, driving high disruption. Demand is moderately elastic because cheaper, faster mapping unlocks new use cases (real-time disaster response, more granular urban planning, location-based services, and more frequent map updates), but total demand is structurally bounded by the finite set of government, engineering, and planning clients that need maps. The role survives but the skill set shifts toward managing AI-driven pipelines, validation, and interpretation rather than manual map construction, fitting the restructure category at disruption >=7 with elasticity of 5-6.

title: Cashiers
rationale: The core work involves physical handling of goods, scanning, bagging, age verification, and in-person customer interaction, which are not directly in AI's path; the main threat is automation via self-checkout and e-commerce rather than AI cognition specifically, so disruption is moderate. Demand for cashier transactions is fixed by retail transaction volume and does not expand if processing becomes cheaper — people don't buy more goods because checkout is faster, so elasticity is very low. Because disruption to the core in-person tasks remains moderate (under 7), this falls into the resilient category, though headcount will continue shrinking due to physical automation rather than AI itself.

title: Chefs and head cooks
rationale: The core work — hands-on cooking, tasting, supervising kitchen staff in a fast-paced physical environment, and maintaining food quality and sanitation — is overwhelmingly physical and presence-based, with AI only touching peripheral tasks like menu planning, recipe ideation, inventory scheduling, and social media marketing. The sense of taste/smell, dexterity, and real-time leadership cannot be automated. Demand for dining out can expand somewhat with rising incomes and lower operational costs, but physical kitchen capacity and the experiential nature of restaurant dining cap how much productivity gains scale headcount down. Because disruption is well below the 7 threshold, this occupation is clearly resilient — AI helps with administration but does not reshape the fundamentally manual, in-person craft.

title: Chemical engineers
rationale: Chemical engineers do significant cognitive work — process design, simulation, cost estimation, and CAD-based modeling — that AI can meaningfully accelerate, but core responsibilities also require physical plant presence, troubleshooting real-world manufacturing processes, ensuring safety compliance, and supervising technicians, keeping disruption moderate rather than high. Demand is fairly inelastic because it depends on physical product manufacturing volumes, capital-intensive plants, and regulatory constraints that don't expand quickly even if engineering analysis becomes cheaper. Since disruption is at or below 6, the occupation is classified as resilient: AI augments the analytical and design portions but does not reshape the hands-on, regulated, plant-bound core of the work.

title: Chemical technicians
rationale: Core work requires hands-on physical presence in laboratories and manufacturing facilities—setting up and maintaining instruments, preparing chemical solutions, monitoring processes, and handling materials—which AI cannot perform directly. AI does assist with the data analysis, reporting, and result interpretation portions, but these are a minority of the daily tasks, keeping disruption moderate. Elasticity is moderate because cheaper analysis could expand testing volume in R&D, environmental monitoring, and quality control, though physical lab throughput and equipment constraints cap growth. Since disruption stays at or below 6, the occupation is resilient: AI augments analytical tasks but the physical, instrument-based core remains human-dependent.

title: Chemists and materials scientists
rationale: A substantial portion of the work — molecular modeling, simulation, data analysis, literature review, and report writing — is highly amenable to AI tools, and AI-driven discovery (e.g., generative chemistry, materials informatics) is already accelerating research. However, the core work still requires hands-on laboratory experimentation, physical sample preparation, instrument operation, and safety-critical handling of substances that AI cannot perform, capping disruption at moderate. Demand is elastic because cheaper, faster discovery unlocks vast latent demand for new drugs, batteries, materials, and chemical processes that are currently bottlenecked by R&D cost and time. Because disruption stays at or below 6 given the irreducible physical/experimental component, the occupation is best classified as resilient — AI augments the analytical periphery while the lab-based core remains human-centered.

title: Childcare workers
rationale: Core tasks—supervising children's safety, feeding, diapering, physical play, and emotional caregiving—are inherently physical, in-person, and require constant human presence and trust, none of which AI can substitute. AI is largely irrelevant to the work beyond peripheral record-keeping or scheduling, so disruption is minimal. Demand is constrained by birth rates and cost barriers that AI cannot meaningfully lower since labor (not technology) is the binding cost, keeping elasticity low. With disruption well below the threshold, this occupation is clearly resilient regardless of elasticity.

title: Chiropractors
rationale: The core work of chiropractic care is fundamentally physical—manual spinal adjustments, palpation, and hands-on manipulation that require dexterity and physical patient presence that AI cannot replicate. AI may assist peripherally with diagnostics (e.g., interpreting x-rays), record-keeping, and treatment planning, but it cannot perform the hands-on adjustments that define the profession. Demand is somewhat elastic given growing interest in non-surgical, drug-free pain management and an aging population, but each session still requires a human practitioner so productivity gains are capped. With disruption well below 6, this occupation is clearly resilient.

title: Civil engineering technologists and technicians
rationale: A substantial portion of the work is digital and cognitive — CAD drafting, cost estimation, data analysis, and report writing — all of which AI tools can materially accelerate, but the occupation also requires significant physical presence for field surveys, site inspections, material/soil testing, and observing construction conformance. This mix caps disruption at moderate since the unpredictable real-world field component cannot be automated. Elasticity is moderate because cheaper engineering support could unlock more infrastructure projects and analysis, but demand is structurally constrained by public budgets, regulatory approval cycles, and the pace of physical construction. With disruption at 6, the core work remains anchored in hands-on, on-site tasks, making the occupation resilient rather than restructured.

title: Civil engineers
rationale: Civil engineers do substantial knowledge work—analysis, CAD design, cost estimation, code research—that AI can meaningfully accelerate, pushing disruption toward the high end. However, core responsibilities include onsite supervision, construction management, regulatory signoff requiring PE licensure, stakeholder coordination, and physical inspection that AI cannot replace, capping disruption at 6. Demand is moderately elastic given strong, funding-dependent infrastructure needs, and cheaper design could unlock more projects, but public budgets and regulatory timelines constrain rapid expansion. Because disruption stays at or below 6, the occupation is resilient: AI reshapes the design and analysis periphery while licensed judgment and field presence remain central.

title: Claims adjusters, appraisers, examiners, and investigators
rationale: Disruption is high because the core work—evaluating claims, reviewing documents, estimating damage costs from photos, checking policy coverage, and flagging fraud—is heavily cognitive, document-based, and rule-driven, all of which AI and automated estimation software already handle well (BLS explicitly notes software can evaluate photos and calculate claim amounts). Some physical inspection and surveillance keeps the score from going higher, but the bulk of adjudication and examination is squarely in AI's path. Elasticity is low because the number of insurance claims is fixed by external events (accidents, disasters, deaths) and regulatory frameworks; cheaper processing does not cause people to file dramatically more legitimate claims, so productivity gains translate directly into fewer workers needed. With high disruption and inelastic demand—reinforced by BLS's projected -5% decline—the occupation fits the replace category.

title: Clinical laboratory technologists and technicians
rationale: The work blends physical specimen handling, sample collection, equipment calibration, and biohazard handling with cognitive analysis and pattern recognition (e.g., examining slides for abnormalities). AI and automated analyzers already augment the diagnostic interpretation and image-reading portions, but the hands-on, in-lab physical tasks and quality assurance keep much of the core human-dependent. Demand has moderate elasticity—an aging population and expanding genetic testing could unlock more testing volume, but lab test demand is largely tied to clinical orders and reimbursement structures, capping runaway expansion. Because disruption sits at moderate (<=6), the occupation is resilient: AI reshapes interpretation workflows and increases automation but does not reshape the core specimen-handling and supervisory work.

title: Coaches and scouts
rationale: Coaching and scouting are predominantly physical, in-person, relationship-driven activities — running practices, motivating athletes, building rapport, and assessing talent live require human presence and interpersonal skill that AI cannot replace. AI does meaningfully assist peripheral tasks like video analysis, performance data tracking, opponent scouting analytics, and identifying prospects, but these augment rather than replace the core hands-on work. Demand could expand moderately as cheaper analytics tools and growing interest in sports instruction unlock more coaching and scouting at amateur levels. With disruption well below the threshold, the occupation is resilient: AI reshapes the analytical tools coaches use but leaves the fundamental human-centered work intact.

title: Community health workers
rationale: The core work is fundamentally human-centered and physical: home visits, building trust with communities, cultural mediation, hands-on outreach, and in-person advocacy. AI can assist with peripheral tasks like recordkeeping, report writing, resource lookup, and data analysis, but cannot replace the interpersonal, culturally-grounded, field-based nature of the role. Demand could expand moderately as healthcare systems extend preventive care to underserved populations, but headcount is largely driven by funding and community need rather than productivity gains. With disruption well below 7, this occupation is resilient—AI touches the administrative periphery but leaves the relational core intact.

title: Compensation and benefits managers
rationale: The core work—analyzing wage data, benchmarking compensation, monitoring regulations, modeling benefits costs, and preparing recommendations—is predominantly cognitive, data-driven, and digital, making it highly susceptible to AI tools that can automate analysis, compliance checks, and reporting. Demand is inelastic because the number of organizations needing a compensation strategy is structurally fixed; cheaper, faster analysis does not cause companies to design dramatically more pay structures, and the BLS already projects 0% growth with functions increasingly outsourced and automated. Since disruption is high (>=7) and elasticity is low (<=4), productivity gains translate into fewer managers needed rather than expanded output, fitting the replace category.

title: Compensation, benefits, and job analysis specialists
rationale: Core tasks—researching compensation trends, performing data and cost analyses, evaluating job descriptions, monitoring regulations, and preparing reports—are almost entirely cognitive, language-based, and data-driven, putting them squarely in AI's path; modern AI tools can already draft job descriptions, analyze salary surveys, and summarize regulatory changes. Demand is structurally inelastic: organizations have a fixed number of positions to classify and benefits plans to administer, and cheaper analysis does not lead companies to consume dramatically more compensation analysis per employee. Productivity gains therefore translate into fewer specialists needed per organization rather than expanded output, fitting the replace category with high disruption (8) and low elasticity (3). The compliance, advisory, and stakeholder-communication aspects provide some buffer, but the bulk of analytical work is highly automatable without offsetting demand growth.

title: Compliance officers
rationale: Compliance work is predominantly knowledge-based: monitoring regulations, drafting policies, conducting audits, documenting findings, and producing reports — all language- and analysis-heavy tasks squarely in AI's path, though human judgment, accountability, and investigations keep it from being fully automatable. Demand elasticity is low because compliance requirements are driven by fixed regulatory obligations rather than price or speed; organizations don't consume more compliance just because it's cheaper, and headcount tends to track regulatory complexity, not productivity. With high disruption (7) and low elasticity (4), AI absorbs much of the routine analysis and documentation while total demand stays roughly flat, producing headcount pressure. The category fits because productivity gains accrue to fewer workers per organization rather than expanded output.

title: Computer and information research scientists
rationale: The work is almost entirely cognitive and digital—algorithm design, coding, experimentation with ML, and writing papers—all directly in AI's path, and AI tools already materially accelerate research and code generation, driving a high disruption score. Elasticity is high because cheaper and faster research output unlocks vast latent demand: AI itself, cybersecurity, data-mining, and new computing paradigms all expand the frontier of problems worth investigating, and these scientists are positioned to wield AI as a force multiplier rather than be replaced by it. Because both disruption and elasticity are high, the occupation fits 'augment'—each researcher becomes dramatically more productive while overall demand grows (BLS projects 20% growth), keeping headcount expanding even as required skills shift toward AI-augmented research.

title: Computer and information systems managers
rationale: The core work is heavily digital and analytical (planning IT strategy, assessing systems, evaluating technology), and AI tools materially assist with analysis, monitoring, and vendor assessment — but the central duties of leadership, decision-making, resource allocation, accountability, and stakeholder coordination remain inherently human and judgment-based, capping disruption at moderate. Demand is highly elastic because cheaper, faster IT capability drives organizations to build more digital infrastructure (cloud, cybersecurity, AI deployment), each of which requires oversight and governance, which is why BLS projects 15% growth. Despite high elasticity, the disruption score of 6 places this in the resilient category: AI augments the analytical periphery but does not reshape the managerial core, and the occupation is positioned to grow as AI adoption itself expands the need for technology leadership.

title: Computer hardware engineers
rationale: Hardware engineering is predominantly digital cognitive work — circuit design, schematic creation, simulation, and test analysis — where AI-assisted EDA tools, automated design verification, and generative chip layout are already materially changing workflows, driving high disruption. However, physical prototyping, manufacturing oversight, and hardware-software co-design retain human-in-the-loop elements that keep it below the maximum. Demand elasticity is high because cheaper, faster hardware design unlocks the proliferation of embedded processors and IoT components across cars, appliances, and medical devices, expanding the total volume of designed products. Because productivity gains are likely absorbed by greatly expanded output rather than headcount cuts, the occupation fits the augment category with stable-to-growing employment per BLS projections.

title: Computer network architects
rationale: The work is predominantly knowledge-based — network design, configuration, documentation, traffic analysis — much of which AI tools can already assist with through automated design optimization, config generation, and predictive monitoring, driving a high disruption score. However, demand is strongly elastic: the explosion of cloud infrastructure, AI workloads, and IoT continuously expands the volume and complexity of networks that must be designed and maintained, and cheaper/faster design unlocks more projects rather than fewer workers. The physical server-room presence, organizational customization, and accountability for mission-critical infrastructure keep humans central. With disruption >=7 and elasticity >=7, productivity gains are absorbed by growing demand, fitting the augment category — each architect produces more while headcount stays stable or grows.

title: Computer programmers
rationale: Disruption is very high because the core work—writing, modifying, and testing code—is exactly what AI code-generation tools already perform well, making this one of the most directly exposed digital occupations. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper code does unlock substantial new software demand, but for this narrowly-defined 'programmer' role (translating designs into code), much of the productivity gain is absorbed by software developers and AI rather than expanding programmer headcount, as reflected in BLS's -6% projection. The combination of disruption >=7 and elasticity 5-6 places this in restructure: the occupation survives but shifts toward higher-level design, system integration, and AI-tool orchestration, with routine coders displaced and adapters moving into developer-style roles.

title: Computer support specialists
rationale: The core work — diagnosing problems, guiding users through troubleshooting steps via chat/phone/email, documenting issues — is highly language- and knowledge-based and directly in the path of AI chatbots and automated diagnostic tools, which BLS already cites as driving employment decline. Demand elasticity is low because IT support demand is largely fixed by the existing installed base of users and devices; cheaper support doesn't meaningfully cause organizations to consume dramatically more troubleshooting, and routine tier-1 tickets are precisely what automation absorbs. With disruption high (8) and elasticity low (4), productivity gains translate into fewer headcount rather than expanded output, consistent with BLS's projected decline; the hands-on hardware setup and complex network troubleshooting portions provide only partial insulation.

title: Computer systems analysts
rationale: Disruption is very high because the core work—analyzing systems, data modeling, programming, writing documentation, testing, and designing improvements—is almost entirely digital and cognitive, placing it squarely in AI's direct path; coding assistants and analytical AI tools already materially accelerate these tasks. Elasticity is high because as digital transformation becomes cheaper and faster, organizations across every sector tend to undertake far more IT modernization, integration, and optimization projects, unlocking substantial latent demand for systems analysis. The combination of high disruption and high elasticity, reinforced by the BLS projection of 9% growth, means productivity gains are largely absorbed by expanded output rather than headcount reduction, so each analyst produces more while overall employment stays stable or grows—fitting the augment category.

title: Concierges
rationale: Much of the informational and booking work (reservations, recommendations, travel arrangements) is digital and increasingly handled by apps and AI assistants, but the core value lies in in-person greeting, physical presence at a front desk, errand-running, package handling, and personalized human hospitality that AI cannot replace. The BLS itself notes hotel concierge roles being automated while residential and senior-living demand grows, which caps but doesn't eliminate the occupation. Demand elasticity is low-to-moderate because these services are tied to physical buildings and resident counts rather than scalable with cheaper output. With disruption at or below 6, the occupation is classified resilient — AI reshapes the informational periphery but the physical, interpersonal core endures.

title: Conservation scientists and foresters
rationale: Disruption is moderate because while AI strongly enhances the analytical portions—GIS mapping, satellite/drone imagery analysis, modeling of fire spread, timber inventory and growth estimation—the core work requires substantial physical field presence: site preparation, controlled burns, fire suppression, walking remote terrain, and in-person negotiation with landowners. Elasticity is moderate as cheaper, faster environmental analysis could unlock more monitoring and conservation planning, but demand is largely driven by public budgets, regulatory mandates, and land area rather than by cost barriers, capping expansion. Because disruption stays at or below 6, the occupation is classified resilient: AI augments the data-heavy peripheral tasks but cannot replace the hands-on, judgment-driven, physically demanding core work.

title: Construction and building inspectors
rationale: Disruption is moderate: while plan review, code compliance checks, report writing, and documentation are increasingly AI-assisted (and remote inspection technology is already cited by BLS as reducing headcount), the core work still requires physical presence to climb, crawl, and use testing equipment at worksites that involve unpredictable real-world conditions. Elasticity is low because demand for inspections is structurally fixed by regulation and the construction cycle—buildings get inspected a set number of times regardless of cost, so cheaper/faster inspection unlocks little latent demand. Because disruption falls at or below 6, the occupation is classified resilient: AI reshapes the documentation and remote-monitoring periphery and may trim some headcount, but the hands-on, code-enforcement core of the job remains human-dependent.

title: Construction equipment operators
rationale: The core work is operating heavy machinery in unpredictable outdoor environments requiring hand-eye-foot coordination, physical presence, equipment maintenance, and real-time crew coordination — tasks that are physical and manual, placing them outside AI's direct path. While GPS guidance and semi-autonomous machinery may augment certain repetitive grading or paving tasks, full autonomy in dynamic construction sites remains distant, so AI touches only the periphery. Demand is tied to infrastructure spending and physical project volume rather than cost-of-cognitive-work, so even efficiency gains wouldn't dramatically expand headcount needs. Because disruption is well below the 6 threshold, this occupation is resilient regardless of elasticity.

title: Construction laborers and helpers
rationale: Disruption is minimal because the core work is entirely physical—hauling materials, digging trenches, operating jackhammers, cleaning sites, and assisting tradesworkers in unpredictable outdoor environments that AI cannot perform. AI is largely irrelevant to daily tasks, with only peripheral effects from prefabrication and robotics that the BLS notes may slightly reduce demand for some helper categories. Elasticity is moderate since construction demand responds to infrastructure investment and cost, but it is capped by physical labor requirements, capital, and permitting rather than AI productivity. With disruption far below 6, this occupation is clearly resilient—AI touches only the edges while the physical core remains firmly human.

title: Construction managers
rationale: Construction managers blend significant knowledge work—cost estimation, scheduling, budgeting, contract interpretation—with irreducible physical, onsite presence: monitoring worksites, coordinating subcontractors, responding to emergencies, and making real-time field judgment calls. AI can materially assist the digital planning, estimating, and scheduling portions, but the core coordination, leadership, and physical oversight of unpredictable real-world job sites cannot be automated, keeping disruption moderate. Demand is fairly elastic given infrastructure needs, energy retrofits, and ongoing population-driven construction, and cheaper planning could unlock more projects. Because disruption stays at or below 6, the occupation is resilient: AI augments the planning toolkit but does not reshape the fundamentally hands-on, presence-dependent nature of the role.

title: Cooks
rationale: Cooking is overwhelmingly physical and manual—preparing, handling, plating food, and operating kitchen equipment in real-world, unpredictable environments where AI software has minimal direct application. Disruption is driven only by peripheral automation in highly standardized fast-food settings (where some headcount decline is projected) and digital ordering systems, leaving the core hands-on work largely untouched. Demand is moderately elastic since cheaper, faster food service does expand dining-out and delivery consumption, which is why restaurant cook employment is projected to grow 15 percent. With disruption well below 6, the occupation is resilient: AI touches only the edges while the manual core endures.

title: Correctional officers and bailiffs
rationale: The core work—guarding inmates, maintaining physical security, restraining individuals, escorting people, and maintaining courtroom order—is inherently physical, requires real-time human presence, and demands judgment in unpredictable, often dangerous situations that AI cannot perform. AI touches only peripheral tasks like report writing, surveillance monitoring, and logging, leaving the central duties essentially unchanged. Demand is inelastic and driven by incarceration rates and criminal justice policy rather than cost or speed of service, and the occupation is actually projected to decline due to sentencing reform and budget constraints unrelated to AI. With disruption well below 6, this occupation is resilient to AI-driven transformation of its core work.

title: Cost estimators
rationale: Cost estimation is predominantly cognitive, data-driven knowledge work—reading documents, analyzing materials/labor costs, running calculations, and preparing reports—all directly in AI's path, with estimation software already boosting productivity per BLS. Demand is relatively inelastic because the number of construction and manufacturing projects requiring estimates is driven by underlying economic activity rather than the cost of estimation itself; cheaper estimating doesn't meaningfully increase how many buildings get built. With disruption at 7 and elasticity around 4, productivity gains translate into fewer estimators needed rather than expanded output, consistent with the BLS-projected employment decline.

title: Court reporters and simultaneous captioners
rationale: The core work—converting speech to accurate text in real time—is squarely in the path of speech-recognition and transcription AI, which has improved dramatically and already handles captioning and much transcription. Demand is largely inelastic: the number of legal proceedings, broadcasts, and CART needs is fixed by court schedules, regulation, and population, so cheaper transcription doesn't meaningfully multiply the volume of proceedings. Some latent demand exists (more captioning of online content, aging population), but courts and regulatory requirements cap growth and AI productivity gains translate primarily into fewer human reporters per output. High disruption with low elasticity yields headcount contraction, fitting replace, even though residual roles for review, certification, and legal-record verification will persist.

title: Craft and fine artists
rationale: This occupation is split between digital illustrators/cartoonists/digital artists whose core work (creating images) is directly in AI's path via generative image tools, and physical craft artists (ceramics, glassblowing, sculpture, jewelry, tattoo, furniture) whose hands-on, material-based work AI cannot perform. The digital subset faces high disruption while the physical and gallery/reputation-driven fine-art market values human authorship and originality, which AI cannot replicate and which buyers specifically pay a premium for. Demand elasticity is moderate: cheaper commercial illustration could expand some volume, but the fine-art and craft market is driven by scarcity, provenance, and human meaning rather than cost or speed, capping expansion. Because overall disruption to the blended occupation sits at the moderate level (much of the core work remains physical or rooted in human authenticity), the resilient category fits—AI reshapes the commercial-illustration periphery without overturning the core craft and fine-art work.

title: Credit counselors
rationale: The core work — gathering financial information, assessing income/debt, calculating repayment plans, budgeting, and preparing written recommendations — is heavily cognitive and language-based, all squarely in AI's path; the BLS itself notes automation software is already making these workers more efficient. The empathetic, rapport-building counseling and creditor negotiation components require human presence, keeping disruption high but not maximal. Demand is moderately elastic: cheaper, faster debt counseling could reach more underserved consumers and expand access, but growth is structurally constrained by the size of the debt-burdened population and existing institutional channels (colleges, credit agencies). With disruption at 7 and elasticity at 5, the occupation survives but shifts toward higher-touch counseling and oversight of AI-driven analysis, displacing those who only perform routine calculations.

title: Customer service representatives
rationale: The core work — answering questions, processing orders, resolving complaints via phone, chat, email, and social media — is almost entirely language-based and digital, placing it squarely in AI's direct path; conversational AI and chatbots already handle a large fraction of routine inquiries today. Demand is inelastic because the number of customer interactions is fixed by the existing customer base and transaction volume; making support 10x cheaper does not cause people to generate dramatically more service requests. With disruption at 9 and elasticity at 2, productivity gains translate directly into headcount reduction, consistent with BLS's projected decline. This is a clear replace case, as automation absorbs the high-volume routine work while only complex inquiries justify human staffing.

title: Dancers and choreographers
rationale: The core work of dancing and choreography is intensely physical, requiring athleticism, live performance, physical stamina, and embodied creativity that AI cannot replicate or perform. AI touches only peripheral aspects like promotion via social media or possibly generating choreographic ideas, but the actual execution and live audience experience are inherently human and bodily. Even if AI lowered production costs, demand for live dance is constrained by funding limits, venue capacity, and the irreplaceable value audiences place on human performers. With disruption far below the threshold, this occupation is clearly resilient regardless of elasticity.

title: Data scientists
rationale: Data science is almost entirely digital and cognitive work — coding, statistical modeling, data cleaning, and visualization — all squarely in AI's path, with AI tools already automating substantial portions of data wrangling, model building, and analysis. However, demand for data-driven insights is heavily suppressed by cost and talent scarcity; cheaper and faster analytics would unlock vast latent demand as more organizations and more datasets get analyzed, consistent with the BLS-projected 34% growth. Because high disruption is paired with high elasticity, productivity gains are absorbed by expanded output rather than headcount cuts, so the role restructures toward AI-augmented work while headcount grows.

title: Database administrators and architects
rationale: Database administration and architecture is almost entirely digital cognitive work — writing SQL, designing schemas, debugging, monitoring performance, and managing security — all squarely in AI's direct path, with cloud automation and AI-assisted tooling already reshaping the routine maintenance portions (reflected in the projected -1% decline for DBAs). Elasticity is moderate: the explosion of AI and data-driven applications creates substantial new demand for well-designed, secure data infrastructure (architects projected +9%), but this demand expansion is partly offset by automation and cloud consolidation that lets fewer people serve more systems. The net effect is restructure because high disruption combines with moderate elasticity, and the field is visibly bifurcating — routine administration shrinks while higher-skill architecture grows, requiring workers to upskill toward design, governance, and AI-data integration roles.

title: Delivery truck drivers and driver/sales workers
rationale: The core work is physically demanding and presence-dependent — loading/unloading cargo, navigating local streets, interacting with customers, and handling last-mile delivery in unpredictable real-world environments that remain very difficult to automate. AI touches only peripheral tasks like route optimization and dispatch logistics, leaving the core work largely intact (autonomous last-mile delivery remains far from practical at scale within 10 years). Demand is highly elastic, driven by e-commerce growth and consumer appetite for faster, cheaper delivery, which is why BLS projects 8% growth. Because disruption is low (<=6), the occupation is resilient regardless of the strong demand tailwinds.

title: Dental and ophthalmic laboratory technicians and medical appliance technicians
rationale: The core work is hands-on physical fabrication—bending, shaping, polishing, and fitting dental appliances, lenses, and prosthetics using tools and materials—which requires manual dexterity and real-world presence that AI cannot replace. AI and adjacent automation (3D printing, CAD design software, automated lens manufacturing) primarily affect the design and digital-workflow portions, somewhat reducing labor needs but not transforming the core craft tasks. Demand is structurally tied to demographic factors (aging population, vision correction, prosthetic needs) and is fairly inelastic to cost/speed gains, with productivity improvements largely absorbed as headcount reductions in dental lab work. Since disruption stays well below the threshold, the occupation is resilient: automation trims the periphery and slows growth, but the hands-on core endures.

title: Dental assistants
rationale: The core work is overwhelmingly physical and hands-on: preparing patients, sterilizing instruments, passing tools during procedures, taking x-rays, and chairside assistance—all requiring direct human presence in tight physical spaces. AI touches only peripheral administrative tasks like scheduling, billing, and recordkeeping, leaving the essential duties unchanged. Demand is moderately constrained by structural factors like an aging population needing more dental care and the regulatory tie to in-office dental procedures, but it cannot dramatically expand from cheaper AI tools since the bottleneck is physical care, not cognitive output. With disruption well below 6, this occupation is resilient—AI augments the back office but does not reshape the hands-on clinical work.

title: Dental hygienists
rationale: Core work is intensely physical and hands-on—removing tartar, polishing teeth, applying sealants in tight spaces requiring fine motor skills and direct patient presence—which AI cannot perform. AI touches only peripheral areas like x-ray analysis, documentation, and care-plan suggestions, leaving the bulk of daily tasks untouched. Demand is somewhat constrained by patient appetite for cleanings, regulatory scope-of-practice limits, and the necessity of in-person procedures, so even cheaper diagnostics wouldn't dramatically expand visits. With disruption well below 6, this occupation is clearly resilient: AI augments diagnostic accuracy at the edges but does not reshape the manual core.

title: Dentists
rationale: Dentistry is fundamentally a hands-on, physical occupation requiring fine motor dexterity, real-time clinical judgment, and direct manipulation inside patients' mouths—tasks AI cannot perform. AI does materially assist peripheral and diagnostic functions (x-ray and imaging analysis, treatment planning, administrative scheduling, and CAD/CAM design of appliances), but the core procedural work remains squarely human. Demand has moderate elasticity since cheaper diagnostics and faster workflows could expand access to underserved populations and cosmetic procedures, but regulatory licensing, the need for in-person care, and physical chair-time fundamentally cap throughput per practitioner. Because disruption stays well below the threshold (most core tasks are untouched), this occupation is resilient—AI augments diagnostics and admin while the manual treatment work endures.

title: Desktop publishers
rationale: Desktop publishing is almost entirely digital, cognitive, and software-based — layout, text formatting, image integration, and file preparation are all squarely in AI's direct path, with generative design tools and automated layout software already performing much of this work.
