Demand is highly inelastic and structurally declining: organizations are shifting to electronic publishing and absorbing these tasks into broader graphic design, web design, and editorial roles, so cheaper/faster output does not unlock new demand for dedicated desktop publishers. With disruption around 9 and elasticity around 2, plus a BLS-projected 12% decline, this fits the replace category — AI absorbs the core work while demand contracts rather than expands.

title: Diagnostic medical sonographers
rationale: The core work involves hands-on physical manipulation of a transducer on patients' bodies, real-time hand-eye coordination, patient positioning, and interpersonal care — tasks AI cannot perform, though AI materially assists with image analysis, abnormality detection, and quality checks. This makes disruption moderate: AI augments the interpretive and documentation portions but the scanning itself requires human presence. Demand elasticity is moderate-to-high because cheaper, AI-assisted imaging combined with an aging population and expanding clinical uses of sonography unlocks meaningful latent demand. Because disruption stays at or below 6 (the manual, in-person scanning core is not reshaped by AI), the occupation is resilient — AI touches the periphery while headcount continues to grow.

title: Diesel service technicians and mechanics
rationale: The core work is overwhelmingly physical—inspecting, disassembling, repairing, and replacing heavy engine components requires dexterity, strength, and hands-on presence that AI cannot perform. AI may assist with diagnostics, technical manual interpretation, and reading electronic control system data, but these are peripheral aids to a manual trade, keeping disruption low. Demand is structurally tied to the existing fleet of diesel vehicles, which is shifting toward electric for short-haul, so productivity gains would not unlock dramatic new demand. With disruption well below 7, this occupation is resilient: AI augments diagnostic steps but does not reshape the fundamentally physical core of the work.

title: Dietitians and nutritionists
rationale: AI can automate meal planning, nutrition analysis, educational content creation, and progress documentation—significant knowledge-work portions—but the core involves face-to-face clinical assessment, counseling, compassion, and team-based care in healthcare settings that require human presence and licensure, capping disruption at moderate. Demand has meaningful expansion potential as cheaper nutrition guidance reaches underserved populations and preventive care grows with an aging population, but clinical and regulatory constraints temper unlimited growth. Because disruption stays at or below 6, the occupation is resilient: AI augments the analytical and administrative periphery while the human counseling core remains intact.

title: Drafters
rationale: Drafting is almost entirely digital, CAD/BIM-based knowledge work that converts specifications into technical drawings—precisely the kind of generative, rule-bound design task AI tools are rapidly automating, driving the high disruption score. Demand is relatively inelastic: the volume of buildings, machines, and infrastructure being designed is constrained by physical construction and manufacturing cycles, capital, and regulation, so faster/cheaper drafting mostly lets engineers and architects absorb the work directly rather than commissioning vastly more drawings. BLS already projects flat-to-declining employment as CAD/BIM lets engineers do drafters' work, confirming productivity gains convert to fewer workers. High disruption combined with low elasticity places this in the replace category.

title: Drywall installers, ceiling tile installers, and tapers
rationale: The core work is almost entirely physical: measuring, cutting, hanging heavy wallboard, taping seams, sanding, and working on ladders, stilts, and scaffolds in unpredictable construction environments. AI has essentially no path to performing these manual tasks and only marginally touches peripheral functions like material estimation, so disruption is minimal. Demand is tied to construction and remodeling cycles and is relatively inelastic to AI-driven productivity gains in office work. With disruption far below the threshold, this occupation is clearly resilient — AI does not reshape the hands-on core of the job.

title: Economists

title: Hand laborers and material movers
rationale: The core work is physical and manual—lifting, moving, packing, cleaning, and bending in unpredictable real-world positions—which AI software cannot perform; disruption comes from physical robotics and warehouse automation rather than AI itself, and even that affects only peripheral and repetitive tasks. Demand is structurally tied to physical volumes of goods, trash, and store traffic, so cheaper handling does not unlock dramatic new latent demand, capping elasticity. Because the disruption score is well below 7, the occupation is resilient: AI touches the periphery (routing, inventory tracking, sorting systems) but does not reshape the hands-on core, and BLS projects modest 4% growth overall.

title: Hazardous materials removal workers
rationale: The core work is intensely physical and hands-on—removing asbestos, lead, and radioactive materials in confined spaces, operating heavy equipment, wearing protective suits, and responding to disaster sites. AI is largely irrelevant to these manual decontamination and removal tasks, touching only peripheral functions like recordkeeping or material identification, so disruption is very low. Demand is structurally constrained by sporadic EPA funding, regulatory schedules, and the fixed inventory of contaminated sites and decommissioning projects, so productivity gains wouldn't unlock large latent demand. Because disruption is well below the threshold, this occupation is resilient: AI affects only the administrative periphery while the physical core remains intact.

title: Health and safety engineers
rationale: The work mixes substantial knowledge tasks (reviewing plans, interpreting regulations, analyzing accident data, drafting safety programs) that AI can meaningfully assist, with critical physical and interpersonal components — site inspections, hazard observation, interviewing employees, and directing installations — that require human presence and judgment. AI accelerates the analytical and documentation portions but cannot independently certify safety or physically inspect facilities, keeping disruption moderate. Demand is structurally constrained by regulatory compliance needs rather than cost-suppressed latent demand, so productivity gains would not dramatically expand headcount (elasticity low). Because disruption stays at or below 6, the occupation is best classified as resilient: AI reshapes the periphery but the core safety-engineering role remains human-anchored.

title: Health education specialists
rationale: Disruption is moderate-to-high: significant portions of the work — developing educational materials, analyzing community health data, writing grant proposals, designing campaigns — are language and cognitive tasks squarely in AI's path, but the core involves community presence, in-person teaching, interpersonal empathy, and trust-building that resist automation. Elasticity is moderate because preventive health education has latent demand (cost reduction in producing materials and programs could expand reach), but growth is structurally constrained by public funding, grant cycles, and the need for human delivery in communities. Since disruption falls at 6 — touching the periphery and material-production tasks but not reshaping the human-centered core — the occupation is best classified as resilient.

title: Health information technologists and medical registrars
rationale: The core work—abstracting clinical data, coding diagnoses, validating data integrity, compiling reports, and maintaining registries—is almost entirely digital, cognitive, and language/classification-based, placing it squarely in AI's direct path; automated coding, NLP-based abstraction, and data validation tools already meaningfully change this work, driving a high disruption score. Elasticity is moderate because the explosive growth of electronic health data creates genuine latent demand for analysis and insight, but regulatory, privacy, and quality-assurance requirements plus the finite scope of registry/reporting tasks cap unbounded expansion. With disruption >=7 and elasticity in the 5-6 range, the occupation survives but shifts: rote abstraction and coding shrink while data analysis, system implementation, validation, and oversight roles grow, rewarding workers who upskill toward analytics and IT governance.

title: Heating, air conditioning, and refrigeration mechanics and installers
rationale: Core HVAC work is overwhelmingly physical and hands-on—installing, repairing, and maintaining equipment in homes and buildings, often in cramped spaces and unpredictable conditions that AI cannot perform. AI touches only peripheral tasks like diagnostics support, record-keeping, scheduling, and load calculations, so disruption to the actual trade is minimal. Demand could grow moderately as energy-efficiency retrofits and smart climate systems increase service needs, but it remains structurally tied to building stock and physical service calls. Because disruption is very low regardless of elasticity, this occupation is clearly resilient.

title: Heavy and tractor-trailer truck drivers
rationale: The core work is physical driving, cargo securing, vehicle inspection, and navigating unpredictable real-world road conditions—tasks that remain heavily dependent on human presence despite high autonomous-vehicle hype. AI may assist with route planning, logging, and partial highway autonomy, but full driverless long-haul operation faces unresolved technical, regulatory, liability, and last-mile challenges within a 10-year window, so AI touches the periphery rather than the core. Freight demand is fairly elastic to lower transport costs since cheaper shipping would expand goods movement, but headcount is tied to physical capacity and the work itself is not yet automatable. With disruption well below 6, this occupation is resilient over the next decade.

title: Heavy vehicle and mobile equipment service technicians
rationale: The core work is highly physical and hands-on—disassembling engines, lifting heavy parts, working in awkward positions on-site—which AI cannot perform. AI assists primarily with computerized diagnostics, which already exist as tools, but the actual repair, recalibration, and reassembly require human dexterity and presence, keeping disruption low. Demand is tied to the physical stock of heavy equipment and is relatively fixed by industry activity rather than suppressed by repair cost, so elasticity is modest. With disruption well below 6, the occupation is resilient: AI touches diagnostics at the periphery but does not reshape the fundamentally manual core.

title: High school teachers
rationale: Disruption is moderate: lesson planning, grading, content generation, and personalized material creation are squarely in AI's path and already being transformed by AI tools, but the core work—classroom management, in-person supervision, behavioral guidance, motivating teenagers, and the custodial/social function of schools—requires sustained human presence and cannot be automated. Elasticity is low because demand for high school teachers is structurally fixed by student enrollment, mandatory schooling laws, fixed classroom ratios, and government budgets rather than by price or speed of instruction; cheaper lesson prep does not create more students. Because disruption is at or below 6, the occupation is classified as resilient: AI will heavily augment the back-office and content tasks of teaching, shifting how teachers spend their time, but it will not reshape the fundamentally human-presence-driven core of the job.

title: Historians
rationale: Historians' core work—researching documents, analyzing and interpreting sources, and writing reports, articles, and books—is overwhelmingly cognitive and language-based, placing it directly in the path of AI tools that excel at synthesizing text, translating foreign-language materials, and drafting narrative, which drives a high disruption score. However, the work also involves physical artifact handling, archival preservation, and public engagement that AI cannot fully replace, tempering the score slightly. Demand is highly inelastic: the field is small (3,400 jobs), funding-constrained, and dependent on donations and public budgets, so cheaper historical analysis does not unlock significantly more consumption of historian services. With high disruption and low elasticity in a structurally constrained, slow-growth field, productivity gains translate to fewer needed workers rather than expanded output, fitting the replace category.

title: Home health and personal care aides
rationale: The core work is overwhelmingly physical and hands-on—bathing, dressing, lifting, transporting, housekeeping, and providing emotional companionship—none of which AI can perform, so disruption is minimal and limited to peripheral admin tasks like scheduling. Demand is highly elastic given the aging population and a structural shift toward home- and community-based care, with much latent demand currently suppressed by cost and labor shortages. Because disruption is well below the threshold of 7, this occupation is classified as resilient: AI touches only the administrative periphery while the demanding physical and interpersonal core remains firmly human.

title: Human resources managers
rationale: HR managers perform substantial knowledge work — drafting policies, screening candidates, analyzing workforce data, ensuring compliance — much of which AI tools can now assist with, pushing disruption to a high-moderate level. However, the core of the role involves interpersonal mediation, leadership, judgment in disputes, strategic consultation with executives, and accountability for legally sensitive decisions, all of which require human presence and trust, keeping disruption from reaching the very high band. Demand elasticity is low because organizations have a structurally bounded need for HR oversight that doesn't scale dramatically with cheaper processing; faster administration mostly means fewer specialists rather than vastly more HR management. Because disruption stays at or below 6 and the human-centered core is not reshaped, the occupation is best classified as resilient — AI augments administrative tasks while the leadership and relationship functions endure.

title: Human resources specialists
rationale: The work is predominantly knowledge- and language-based: screening resumes, drafting job postings, answering policy questions, processing paperwork, and maintaining records — all tasks where AI tools (resume parsing, chatbots, automated scheduling, generative drafting) are already materially deployed, driving a high disruption score. Demand is relatively inelastic because the number of HR specialists is tethered to organizational headcount and hiring volume rather than to the cost of HR processing; cheaper, faster HR work does not cause companies to hire dramatically more people or run vastly more HR functions, so productivity gains largely reduce required staff. While interpersonal and judgment-heavy elements (dispute resolution, in-person interviewing, strategic planning) provide some resilience, much routine specialist work is automatable and demand won't expand enough to absorb the efficiency gains, fitting the replace category despite modest projected growth.

title: Hydrologists
rationale: Hydrologists do substantial computer modeling, data analysis, forecasting, and report writing — all directly in AI's path — which pushes disruption upward, but core duties also require fieldwork (measuring streamflow, collecting water/soil samples, hiking to remote sites) that AI cannot perform, keeping disruption at moderate. Demand is largely driven by government budgets, regulatory requirements, and finite water-management projects, so cheaper analysis does not unlock dramatically more consumption, yielding low elasticity. Because the disruption score sits at 6 with a meaningful physical/field component, the occupation is best classified as resilient: AI will accelerate the analytical and modeling portions but cannot reshape the core mixed-field role.

title: Industrial designers
rationale: The conceptual, digital core of industrial design—sketching, rendering, 3D CAD modeling, generating design alternatives—sits directly in the path of generative AI tools that can already produce concepts and iterate designs rapidly, driving high disruption; however, physical prototyping, materials/manufacturing feasibility, client consultation, and engineering collaboration retain meaningful human presence. Demand is moderately elastic: cheaper, faster design iteration could expand the number of products that get professionally designed and unlock more customized or niche products, but growth is capped by manufacturing economics, declining domestic manufacturing employment, and the fixed pace at which physical products reach market. With disruption at 7 and elasticity at 6, the occupation fits restructure—designers will shift toward AI-augmented concept curation, manufacturing integration, and client-facing roles while routine modeling work shrinks, rewarding those who adapt and displacing those who don't.

title: Industrial engineering technologists and technicians
rationale: The disruption score is moderate because a significant portion of work involves data analysis, statistical studies, CAD/CAM design, and workflow planning that AI can materially assist with, but the core role requires physical presence at manufacturing sites to conduct time-and-motion studies, observe operations, and collect floor-level data. The elasticity score is moderate because cheaper, faster process optimization could expand demand as more facilities pursue efficiency gains and automation support, but manufacturing-specific demand is structurally constrained by physical capacity and capital investment cycles. Since disruption falls at or below 6 and the work fundamentally depends on on-site observation and team collaboration with engineers, AI reshapes the analytical periphery without replacing the embodied, location-bound core, making the occupation resilient.

title: Industrial engineers
rationale: Industrial engineers do substantial data analysis, process design, simulation, and optimization that AI tools can materially accelerate, but the core work also requires on-site observation of physical systems, cross-departmental collaboration, and judgment about real-world manufacturing and service environments, capping disruption at moderate. Demand elasticity is high because efficiency optimization is a cost-reduction function whose value scales with cheaper analysis—more companies and processes (in healthcare, logistics, automation) become worth optimizing as the cost drops. Since disruption falls at or below 6 with significant physical and presence-based components, the occupation is best classified as resilient: AI augments the analytical periphery but does not reshape the hands-on, collaborative core, and BLS projects above-average growth.

title: Industrial machinery mechanics, machinery maintenance workers, and millwrights
rationale: Core work is hands-on physical repair, installation, and disassembly of industrial machinery requiring manual dexterity, on-site presence, and unpredictable real-world troubleshooting that AI cannot perform directly. AI primarily augments the peripheral diagnostic side via predictive maintenance and vibration analysis, which improves scheduling efficiency but does not replace the physical repair tasks. Demand is moderately elastic as automated manufacturing expands and more machines require upkeep, supporting the projected 13% growth. Because disruption is low (≤6), the occupation is resilient — AI touches diagnostics but the physical core remains firmly human.

title: Industrial production managers
rationale: The disruption score is moderate because while data analysis, scheduling, production planning, and quality reporting are increasingly augmented by AI, the core of the role requires physical presence on the plant floor, real-time problem-solving with equipment and people, and human leadership/coordination across departments that AI cannot replace. Elasticity is low because manufacturing output is constrained by physical capacity, capital, and demand for goods rather than by the cost of management oversight—cheaper management coordination does not unlock proportionally more plants to manage. Since disruption sits at or below 6, the occupation is resilient: AI will streamline the analytical and reporting tasks but the on-site supervisory, leadership, and operational decision-making core remains firmly human.

title: Information clerks
rationale: Core tasks—data entry, record maintenance, answering routine inquiries, processing forms and orders—are predominantly digital, language-based, and rule-following, placing them squarely in AI's direct path; chatbots, self-service portals, and document automation already replace much of this work. Demand is largely fixed: the volume of records to file, licenses to issue, or orders to process does not expand meaningfully when the work becomes cheaper, so productivity gains convert directly into fewer workers rather than more output. With disruption around 8 and elasticity around 2, this fits 'replace,' consistent with BLS projections of overall decline and steep drops in order clerks, file clerks, and interviewers. Some physical/in-person subsegments (hotel desk, ticket agents handling luggage) are more resilient, but the occupation as a whole faces headcount contraction.

title: Information security analysts
rationale: The work is almost entirely digital and cognitive—monitoring networks, analyzing logs, detecting vulnerabilities, writing reports—all directly in AI's path, and AI-driven threat detection tools already materially change daily workflows, driving a high disruption score. However, the threat landscape expands as attackers also weaponize AI, so cheaper/faster defensive capability unlocks vastly more demand: more systems, more attack surfaces, and more frequent threats all require coverage. Because demand for security scales with the growth of digital systems and adversarial sophistication, productivity gains get absorbed by more security work rather than headcount cuts, fitting the augment category.

title: Instructional coordinators
rationale: Much of the work—curriculum development, analyzing test data, reviewing educational materials, designing training—is knowledge and language-based, so AI can meaningfully assist with drafting curricula, summarizing data, and generating instructional content. However, core tasks like observing teachers, mentoring, building relationships with staff, and navigating school board/regulatory politics require human presence and judgment, capping disruption at moderate. Demand is structurally constrained by state and local education budgets and fixed numbers of schools, so cheaper curriculum work would not dramatically expand headcount. With disruption at 6 and elasticity low, the occupation fits 'resilient' since AI augments peripheral knowledge tasks without reshaping the relational, supervisory core.

title: Insulation workers
rationale: The core work is almost entirely physical: measuring, cutting, fitting, stapling, and spraying insulation in walls, attics, and around pipes, often in confined spaces or at heights. AI is largely irrelevant to these hands-on tasks, touching only peripheral functions like blueprint review or material estimation. Demand is tied to construction cycles, energy efficiency retrofits, and physical building stock, so it cannot dramatically expand from cheaper cognitive work. With disruption far below the threshold, this occupation is clearly resilient to AI.

title: Insurance sales agents
rationale: The work is predominantly cognitive and language-based — explaining policies, analyzing client needs, comparing options, processing sales and renewals, and maintaining records — all tasks AI tools can already largely automate or assist, with online self-service and AI advisors directly substituting for the agent's information-brokerage role. Demand elasticity is low because insurance purchasing is largely mandated or need-driven (people buy what they're legally required or what protects existing assets), so cheaper/faster service does not meaningfully expand the number of policies sold; lower cost mostly translates to fewer agents per transaction. The relationship-building and trust elements provide some buffer in complex commercial and life segments, but the bulk of routine personal-lines work faces direct displacement, fitting the replace category with disruption >= 7 and elasticity <= 4.

title: Insurance underwriters
rationale: Underwriting is almost entirely digital, rules-based risk analysis that already relies heavily on automated software to score applications and recommend premiums — exactly the kind of cognitive, data-driven work in AI's direct path, so disruption is very high. Demand for insurance underwriting is fixed by the number of applications and policies sold; making it 10x cheaper doesn't generate dramatically more policies needing review, so productivity gains convert directly to fewer workers (elasticity is very low, consistent with BLS's projected -3% decline). With disruption >= 7 and elasticity <= 4, this fits the replace category: AI absorbs the core decision-making while total demand stays flat, driving headcount contraction.

title: Interior designers
rationale: Much of interior design work is digital and cognitive — CAD/BIM modeling, generating visualizations, mood boards, material specs, cost estimates, and layout iterations — all of which generative AI tools can now accelerate dramatically, driving a high disruption score. However, core elements like client relationship-building, site visits, on-site coordination with contractors, taste/judgment, and physical installation oversight remain human-anchored. Demand is moderately elastic: cheaper, faster visualization unlocks more renovation and design services for clients who previously couldn't afford bespoke design, but the market remains constrained by the physical, relationship-driven, and project-management nature of the work. With disruption at 7 and elasticity at 6, the occupation survives but skill sets shift toward AI-assisted design curation, client management, and project execution, fitting restructure.

title: Interpreters and translators
rationale: Translation is one of the most directly AI-exposed language tasks; machine translation and CAT tools already handle large fractions of written translation, with human work increasingly shifting to post-editing, and AI speech translation is rapidly improving on the interpreting side. While certain segments (legal/medical interpreting, sign language, in-person liaison, high-stakes cultural adaptation) retain genuine human value, the core text-conversion work is squarely in AI's path, pushing disruption high. Demand elasticity is limited: cheaper translation does unlock some latent multilingual content needs, but much demand is fixed by specific events, legal requirements, and human-presence settings, so productivity gains largely substitute for headcount rather than expanding output proportionally. With high disruption and low-to-moderate elasticity capped around 4, the occupation faces net contraction in the routine portions, fitting the replace category despite resilient niches.

title: Ironworkers
rationale: Ironworking is almost entirely physical and performed in unpredictable outdoor, high-elevation environments requiring strength, balance, hand-eye coordination, and real-time judgment—core tasks far outside AI's direct reach, so disruption is minimal. Demand is tied to physical construction of buildings, bridges, and infrastructure, which is constrained by capital, permitting, and material costs rather than the cost of cognitive labor, making elasticity low-to-moderate. Because disruption is well below the threshold, the occupation is resilient: AI may aid peripheral tasks like blueprint generation or rigging calculations, but the hands-on erection and welding of steel remains firmly human.

title: Janitors and building cleaners
rationale: The core work—sweeping, mopping, cleaning restrooms, emptying trash, minor repairs, and snow removal—is almost entirely physical and requires unpredictable real-world navigation, so AI is largely irrelevant to daily tasks. Robotic cleaning equipment may assist with some floor tasks but cannot handle the varied, dexterous, and judgment-based duties across diverse environments. Demand for clean spaces is relatively fixed and tied to existing building footprints, so cheaper cleaning would not dramatically expand consumption. With disruption far below the threshold, this occupation is clearly resilient.

title: Jewelers and precious stone and metal workers
rationale: The core work is highly physical and dexterity-based — soldering, setting stones, polishing, hand engraving, and repair require manual craftsmanship and human presence at a workbench, so AI touches only peripheral tasks like CAD design, cost estimation, and gemstone grading documentation. While CAD/CAM and 3D printing already assist design and prototyping, the hands-on assembly and repair work remains firmly human. Demand is structurally constrained by the discretionary, luxury nature of jewelry and is also being eroded by imports, so cheaper production would not dramatically expand the US workforce. Because disruption stays low (under 6), the occupation is resilient — AI affects the periphery but does not reshape the manual craft at its core.

title: Judges and hearing officers
rationale: The core tasks—researching legal issues, reading documents, writing opinions—are cognitive and language-based, where AI tools can materially assist with research, drafting, and document review. However, the defining function of judging is the legitimate exercise of legal authority, discretion, and judgment, which is constitutionally and procedurally reserved for human officials and cannot be delegated to AI, capping disruption at moderate. Demand is structurally inelastic: caseloads are bounded by litigation volume and government budgets rather than by the cost or speed of judicial work, so productivity gains would not expand headcount. Because disruption stays at or below 6, the occupation is resilient—AI augments research and administrative tasks but does not reshape the human core of adjudication.

title: Kindergarten and elementary school teachers
rationale: Core work involves in-person supervision, behavioral management, hands-on instruction, and emotional/developmental care of young children—tasks that require physical presence and human relationship-building that AI cannot replace. AI meaningfully assists peripheral tasks like lesson planning, grading, parent communication, and generating teaching materials, but the central classroom role remains human-driven, keeping disruption moderate. Elasticity is low because demand is structurally fixed by student enrollment, compulsory schooling mandates, mandated student-teacher ratios, and government budgets rather than by cost or speed of instruction. Since disruption stays at or below 6, the occupation is resilient: AI augments teacher productivity at the margins but does not reshape the fundamental supervisory and instructional core.

title: Labor relations specialists
rationale: Much of the work is document drafting, policy development, compliance review, and research that AI can materially assist (contract drafting, grievance documentation, labor law analysis), pushing disruption toward high—but the core involves face-to-face negotiation, building rapport, navigating tense interpersonal disputes, and trust-based mediation that resist automation, keeping it at moderate (6). Demand is highly inelastic: it is tied to union membership rates and the fixed number of collective bargaining relationships, which are flat-to-declining rather than cost-suppressed; cheaper labor relations work would not generate dramatically more contracts or grievances. Because disruption stays at or below 6, the occupation is classified resilient—AI augments the documentation and analysis periphery but the relationship-driven, presence-based negotiation core remains human.

title: Landscape architects
rationale: Much of the design work—CADD modeling, site plans, cost estimates, graphic representations, and analysis of environmental/GIS data—is digital and cognitive, putting a substantial portion of tasks in AI's path and warranting a moderate-to-high disruption score. However, the core work still requires creative vision, client collaboration, on-site inspection, physical judgment about real terrain, and licensure-protected professional accountability, which keeps disruption from reaching the very-high tier. Demand has moderate elasticity: cheaper, faster design could unlock more green infrastructure, residential, and restoration projects, but growth is constrained by construction budgets, land availability, and regulatory cycles. Because disruption stays at or below the 6 threshold and the human-presence and licensure components remain central, the occupation is best classified as resilient.

title: Lawyers
rationale: Legal work is predominantly cognitive and language-based — research, document drafting, contract review, and analysis are all directly in AI's path, and tools like generative AI and e-discovery already materially change legal workflows, driving a high disruption score. Demand elasticity is constrained because most legal demand is gated by courts, regulation, licensing requirements, and the fixed number of disputes and transactions; while cheaper legal services would unlock some latent demand (small businesses, underserved individuals), structural and regulatory caps keep elasticity low-to-moderate. With disruption >= 7 and elasticity <= 4, the net effect is replace: AI absorbs much of the routine drafting and research work without proportional demand expansion, leading firms to restaff leaner and contract headcount in junior/associate roles, consistent with BLS noting routine work automation and price-competitive staffing changes.

title: Librarians and library media specialists
rationale: The information-retrieval, research-assistance, and cataloging core of librarianship is highly knowledge- and language-based, and AI tools (search, summarization, automated cataloging) already materially change how reference and discovery work is done, pushing disruption toward high. However, much of the role centers on in-person services, public programming, teaching, community engagement, school media instruction, and curation tied to physical settings and institutional budgets, which AI cannot displace, keeping disruption at a moderate 6. Demand is largely fixed by public funding, school mandates, and institutional structures rather than by the cost or speed of information lookup, so cheaper AI does not unlock large new demand for librarians (elasticity ~4). Because disruption is at or below the 6 threshold and a substantial portion of work is human-presence-dependent, the occupation is best classified as resilient.

title: Library technicians and assistants
rationale: The work mixes physical tasks (shelving, handling materials, staffing desks) with digital, cognitive tasks (cataloguing, database maintenance, answering reference questions) that AI can increasingly automate, placing disruption at the upper end of moderate. However, the physical and in-person service components anchor it below the high-disruption threshold. Demand is highly inelastic—library use is declining and constrained by public budgets, so cheaper information retrieval does not expand headcount needs (the occupation is already projected to shrink 7%). With disruption at 6 and falling on the boundary, the occupation classifies as resilient since AI touches the periphery and digital tasks but the core in-person and physical work remains, though slow contraction continues for budgetary rather than AI-replacement reasons.

title: Licensed practical and licensed vocational nurses
rationale: Core LPN/LVN tasks are overwhelmingly physical and hands-on—monitoring vital signs, changing bandages, bathing and feeding patients, collecting samples, and providing bedside comfort that requires direct human presence. AI touches only peripheral tasks like documentation and health-record maintenance, leaving the bulk of daily work untouched. Demand is structurally elastic given aging demographics and rising chronic conditions, but this work cannot be made dramatically cheaper or faster by AI because it is constrained by physical labor and licensing. Since disruption is well below the threshold of 7, the occupation is resilient: AI assists with documentation but does not reshape the fundamentally physical, care-based core.

title: Loan officers
rationale: The core work—gathering and verifying financial information, running underwriting, assessing creditworthiness, and reviewing compliance—is largely digital, data-driven, and increasingly automated; underwriting software already does much of the analysis and AI can extend this to document verification, risk scoring, and even applicant interaction. Demand elasticity is low because lending volume is constrained by macroeconomic conditions, interest rates, and regulatory limits rather than the cost or speed of loan processing; cheaper underwriting does not dramatically expand the number of loans people take out. While relationship-building and sales (especially commercial/mortgage) provide some human resilience, the underwriting and consumer segments are highly automatable. With disruption high and demand inelastic, productivity gains convert to headcount stagnation/contraction, fitting the replace category, consistent with BLS's slower-than-average outlook.

title: Lodging managers
rationale: The disruption score is moderate because while AI can automate scheduling, revenue management, reservations, billing, and demand forecasting, the core of the job requires physical presence, on-site inspection of rooms and grounds, in-person guest interaction, staff supervision, and real-time problem resolution that cannot be delegated to software. Demand elasticity is low because the number of lodging facilities is structurally fixed by physical real estate and travel volumes; cheaper management does not cause people to build dramatically more hotels or take more trips, and short-term rentals already cap growth. Because disruption stays at or below 6, the occupation is resilient—AI tools will streamline back-office and analytical tasks but will not reshape the fundamentally on-premise, interpersonal core of the manager role.

title: Logging workers
rationale: Logging work is overwhelmingly physical—felling trees, operating heavy machinery, hauling logs in remote and hazardous outdoor terrain—tasks that require human presence and dexterity AI cannot replace. AI may marginally assist log grading/scaling and route or harvest planning, but these are peripheral to the core manual work, keeping disruption very low. Demand for timber is structurally constrained by housing markets, raw material needs, and environmental regulation, so cheaper output would unlock only limited additional consumption. With disruption well below 6, this occupation is resilient; mechanization rather than AI continues to be the primary driver of the modest projected headcount decline.

title: Logisticians
rationale: Logistics is predominantly knowledge work — forecasting, demand-supply alignment, route optimization, inventory analysis, and software management — all of which are squarely in AI's path, with optimization and forecasting tools already materially reshaping the role, justifying a high disruption score. Demand elasticity is moderate: cheaper, faster logistics analysis unlocks more granular supply-chain optimization and supports the expanding complexity of e-commerce, but total demand is anchored to physical goods movement and organizational scale rather than near-unlimited latent demand. The combination of high disruption and moderate elasticity fits restructure — the occupation persists and even grows per BLS projections, but the skill set shifts toward overseeing AI-driven optimization systems, exception handling, and supplier/customer liaison rather than manual analysis.

title: Machinists and tool and die makers
rationale: The core work is physical and hands-on: setting up, operating, and disassembling machine tools, aligning workpieces to tolerances of .0001 inch, polishing surfaces, and physically verifying parts. AI assists meaningfully in the digital portions—CAD/CAM design, CNC programming, and blueprint interpretation—but the manual dexterity, machine setup, and shop-floor presence cannot be automated by AI alone (that requires expensive robotics, not just software). Demand is constrained by overall manufacturing volume and reshoring trends rather than software cost, so productivity gains modestly reduce headcount rather than unlocking large latent demand. Because disruption stays at or below the moderate range (core work remains physical), this occupation is resilient even though some tasks like CNC programming face AI pressure.

title: Management analysts
rationale: Disruption is high because the core work — gathering and organizing data, analyzing financial reports, developing recommendations, and writing reports/presentations — is predominantly cognitive and language-based, all directly in AI's path; current LLMs already accelerate analysis, synthesis, and deliverable creation. However, key elements like client relationships, onsite observation, stakeholder trust, and change-management persuasion still require human presence, keeping it below the 8-9 range. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper, faster consulting unlocks meaningful latent demand among smaller firms and government agencies seeking efficiency gains, but total demand is somewhat capped by the relationship-driven, trust-based nature of high-stakes advisory work. The combination of disruption >=7 and elasticity in the 5-6 band fits restructure — the analyst role survives but shifts toward judgment, client management, and AI-tool orchestration, displacing those who only do routine analysis.

title: Manicurists and pedicurists
rationale: The core work is entirely physical and hands-on—cleaning, shaping, polishing nails and massaging hands and feet—requiring fine dexterity, real-world presence, and direct client interaction that AI cannot perform. AI is irrelevant to the core service and touches only peripheral tasks like salon scheduling, inventory, or booking. Demand is somewhat constrained but already grows steadily as a low-cost luxury, and AI productivity gains don't apply since the bottleneck is human manual labor, not cognitive cost. With disruption far below the threshold, this occupation is clearly resilient regardless of elasticity.

title: Marine engineers and naval architects
rationale: A substantial portion of the work—design, CAD drafting, simulation, structural analysis, cost estimation, technical reporting—is digital and increasingly aided by AI design and modeling tools, pushing disruption toward the high end. However, the core work involves significant physical presence (shop floors, sea trials, offshore rigs, prototype testing), regulatory coordination, and PE-licensed accountability that AI cannot replace, capping disruption at 6. Demand has moderate latent upside from emissions-driven ship redesign and offshore wind expansion, but the field is small and constrained by heavy capital costs and regulation, so cheaper design doesn't dramatically multiply vessels built. Because disruption stays at or below 6 with the human-presence and licensing core intact, this occupation is resilient—AI augments the engineering analysis but does not reshape the fundamental role.

title: Market research analysts
rationale: The core work—gathering data, analyzing with statistical software, forecasting trends, and producing reports, charts, and presentations—is almost entirely digital and cognitive, placing it directly in AI's path; modern LLMs and analytics tools already automate much of the data synthesis, visualization, and report-writing. Demand is moderately elastic: cheaper, faster analysis enables more businesses (especially smaller ones) to access market research and supports the growing use of big data across industries, but core demand is partly capped by the number of products, campaigns, and strategic decisions needing analysis. With disruption high (8) and elasticity in the moderate range (6), the occupation survives but the skill set shifts toward overseeing AI tools, interpreting outputs, and strategic judgment rather than manual data crunching—classic restructure territory.

title: Marriage and family therapists
rationale: The core work of marriage and family therapy depends on human empathy, building rapport, reading emotional cues, and navigating complex relational dynamics in real time—tasks AI cannot meaningfully replicate. AI touches only peripheral functions like documentation, scheduling, insurance billing, and possibly some preliminary screening, keeping disruption moderate-to-low. Demand for mental health services is heavily suppressed by cost, stigma, and access, so cheaper supporting tools could expand reach, but the human therapeutic relationship remains irreplaceable. Because disruption is well below the threshold (4), the occupation is resilient: AI augments administrative tasks but does not reshape the core relational work.

title: Masonry workers
rationale: Masonry work is almost entirely physical and hands-on—laying brick, mixing mortar, cutting stone, finishing concrete—requiring dexterity, strength, and unpredictable real-world job-site presence that AI cannot perform. AI is irrelevant to the core craft and touches only peripheral tasks like blueprint interpretation or material estimation, so disruption is minimal. Demand is tied to overall construction activity and is structurally constrained (slow 2% projected growth, with prefab panels and substitute materials actually reducing some demand), so elasticity is low. With disruption far below the threshold, the occupation is clearly resilient—AI may slightly assist planning but will not reshape the manual labor at its center.

title: Massage therapists
rationale: The core work is entirely physical—manipulating soft tissues and joints by hand requires dexterity, strength, and human touch that AI cannot replicate; only peripheral tasks like scheduling, notes, and marketing are digitizable. Demand could expand somewhat with wellness trends and growing acceptance of massage for pain management, but the service is fundamentally capped by the need for one human therapist per client per session, so productivity cannot scale via AI. With disruption far below the threshold, this occupation is clearly resilient—AI touches only administrative edges while the hands-on core remains untouched.

title: Material moving machine operators
rationale: The core work is physical operation of forklifts, cranes, conveyors, and dredges requiring real-time spatial coordination, hand-eye control, and presence in unpredictable physical environments — tasks largely outside AI's direct path. AI and automation (robotic forklifts, automated guided vehicles, sensors) do threaten warehouse/conveyor segments, but adoption is gradual, capital-intensive, and complementary rather than fully replacing operators in the near term. Demand is tied to physical volume of goods moved, which expands modestly with e-commerce but is structurally constrained rather than cost-suppressed latent demand. With disruption well below 7, this occupation is resilient: AI/automation touches efficiency and some routine indoor tasks but does not reshape the hands-on core within the decade.

title: Material recording clerks
rationale: The core work — recordkeeping, inventory tracking, compiling reports, scheduling, and verifying shipments — is predominantly digital and data-driven, directly in AI's path, with RFID, automated storage/retrieval, and AI-driven inventory systems already replacing manual counting and recordkeeping (driving the high disruption score). Demand for inventory tracking is structurally fixed: businesses need accurate records regardless of cost, and cheaper/faster recordkeeping does not cause companies to track dramatically more inventory, so productivity gains convert directly to fewer workers (low elasticity). With disruption at 7 and elasticity at 2, plus BLS already projecting a 6% decline driven by automation, this fits the replace category — significant headcount contraction as automated systems absorb the core tasks.

title: Materials engineers
rationale: Materials engineering is heavily computational and increasingly relies on machine learning for materials discovery, property prediction, and simulation — AI tools like generative materials models are already transforming this work, driving a high disruption score. However, core tasks still require physical experimentation, lab testing, failure analysis, and validation that cannot be fully automated. Demand is moderately elastic: cheaper, faster materials discovery would accelerate development of new alloys, polymers, and semiconductors, expanding R&D scope, but adoption is constrained by capital-intensive manufacturing, regulatory qualification cycles, and the small specialized workforce. With disruption at 7 and elasticity at 6, the occupation survives but shifts toward AI-augmented computational design and validation, displacing those who don't adapt while rewarding those who master ML-driven workflows.

title: Mathematicians and statisticians
rationale: The core work — data analysis, statistical modeling, writing code, designing experiments, and interpreting results — is almost entirely digital and cognitive, placing it directly in AI's path; modern AI and statistical software already materially accelerate these tasks, driving a high disruption score. Demand elasticity is high because the explosion of digitally stored data and the falling cost of analysis unlocks substantial latent demand: more businesses, healthcare entities, and policymakers will want rigorous statistical insight when it becomes faster and cheaper. Because heavy disruption pairs with strong demand expansion (and BLS already projects much-faster-than-average growth for statisticians), each worker becomes more productive while headcount stays stable or grows, fitting the augment category rather than replacement.

title: Mechanical engineering technologists and technicians
rationale: The work mixes substantial digital/cognitive tasks (3D CAD modeling, drawings, data analysis, calculations, reporting) that AI can increasingly assist or automate, with hands-on physical tasks like setting up tests, assembling mechanical parts, operating machinery, and troubleshooting equipment on factory floors. AI strongly disrupts the design and analysis portion but the physical fabrication, installation, and real-world testing components keep disruption at the high-moderate boundary. Demand elasticity is moderate—cheaper, faster engineering support could enable more product development and prototyping, but employment is structurally tied to manufacturing capacity and engineering team needs rather than purely cost-suppressed latent demand. With disruption at 6, the core role still requires significant physical presence and hands-on skill, so it qualifies as resilient rather than restructure.

title: Mechanical engineers
rationale: Mechanical engineering is heavily knowledge-based — CAD design, simulation, analysis, and specification generation are all directly in AI's path, and generative design tools already materially accelerate these tasks, driving a high disruption score. However, core work still requires physical prototyping, worksite presence, integration of real hardware, and licensed professional judgment, capping disruption below the very-high range. Demand is elastic because cheaper, faster design unlocks more product iterations, more complex automation integration, and more devices being engineered across industries — design capacity is currently cost- and time-constrained. With disruption at 7 and elasticity at 7, productivity gains are likely absorbed by expanded output rather than headcount reduction, fitting the augment category.

title: Medical and health services managers
rationale: Much of the work — budgeting, scheduling, reporting, records management, compliance monitoring — is cognitive and digital, and AI tools can materially streamline these administrative tasks, pushing disruption toward moderate-high. However, the core of the job involves human leadership, staff supervision, regulatory navigation, on-site facility oversight, and interpersonal coordination with physicians and patients that AI cannot replace, keeping disruption at 6. Demand elasticity is moderate because an aging population and increasing healthcare complexity drive structural growth, and any productivity gains tend to be absorbed by expanded oversight needs rather than headcount cuts. Because disruption is at or below 6, the occupation is best classified as resilient — AI reshapes administrative tasks but does not transform the managerial core.

title: Medical assistants
rationale: Medical assistants split time between hands-on clinical tasks (taking vitals, drawing blood, giving injections, prepping patients) which require physical presence, and administrative/cognitive tasks (scheduling, coding, records entry, insurance billing) which AI can meaningfully assist. The physical and patient-facing clinical work anchors the role and keeps disruption moderate, even as AI streamlines the back-office portion. Demand is structurally expanding due to an aging population and broader healthcare access, and lower administrative costs could free assistants to support more patients. Because disruption stays at or below 6, the occupation is resilient—AI reshapes the administrative periphery but does not displace the core hands-on, in-person work.

title: Medical dosimetrists
rationale: Disruption is high because the core work—calculating radiation doses, designing treatment plans from CT/MRI scans, and performing QA on equipment—is heavily computational and image-based, exactly the kind of optimization and pattern-recognition task where AI/treatment-planning algorithms are already making rapid inroads. Elasticity is low because demand for radiation oncology is driven by cancer incidence and physician prescriptions, not by the cost or speed of dose planning; cheaper planning won't cause patients to receive dramatically more treatment, and the field is tightly regulated and physician-gated. With disruption >=7 and elasticity <=4, productivity gains from AI are likely to be absorbed by fewer dosimetrists per clinic rather than by expanded volume, fitting the replace category—though the small workforce and physician oversight/safety requirements may slow headcount contraction.

title: Medical equipment repairers
rationale: The core work is hands-on physical repair, installation, and calibration of medical equipment requiring dexterity, physical stamina, on-site presence, and mechanical troubleshooting—tasks AI cannot perform directly. AI may assist with diagnostics, predictive maintenance scheduling, technical manual lookup, and software/cybersecurity tasks, but these are peripheral to the physical work. Demand is moderately elastic, driven by growth in medical equipment volume from chronic disease prevalence and an aging population rather than by AI cost reductions. Since disruption is low (≤6), this occupation is resilient: AI augments diagnostics but does not reshape the physically grounded core work.

title: Medical records specialists
rationale: The work is almost entirely digital and cognitive — reviewing records, assigning standardized codes, data entry, and retrieval — all squarely in AI's path, and AI-powered coding tools are already being adopted as noted in the BLS outlook itself. Demand is structurally fixed: the volume of patient records to be coded is determined by healthcare utilization, not by the cost or speed of coding, so productivity gains translate directly into fewer workers per record rather than vastly more coding output. With high disruption (9) and inelastic demand (2), this fits the replace category; even modest population-driven volume growth is likely to be more than offset by per-worker productivity gains from AI.

title: Medical scientists
rationale: Disruption is high because much of medical research—hypothesis generation, data analysis, literature review, experimental design, grant and paper writing—is cognitive and increasingly accelerated by AI tools that can model proteins, predict drug interactions, and analyze trial data far faster than humans; however, the wet-lab experimentation, clinical trial supervision, and physical sample handling keep it below the very-high tier. Elasticity is high because demand for medical research is enormous and currently bottlenecked by cost and speed: cheaper, faster discovery would unlock vastly more research into diseases, drug candidates, and personalized therapies rather than satisfy a fixed quota of studies. With disruption >= 7 and elasticity >= 7, productivity gains are absorbed by expanded research output, so headcount stays stable or grows while each scientist becomes dramatically more productive, fitting the augment category.

title: Medical transcriptionists
rationale: The work is entirely digital language processing—converting voice to text and editing—which is squarely in the direct path of speech recognition and NLP models that already produce high-quality drafts. The disruption score is very high because AI ambient documentation tools increasingly let physicians document encounters in real time, eliminating the transcription step entirely. Demand is highly inelastic: the volume of medical documentation is fixed by the number of patient encounters, so making transcription cheaper does not generate more reports—it simply requires fewer workers. With very high disruption and near-zero elasticity, headcount contracts, matching the BLS-projected decline.

title: Meeting, convention, and event planners
rationale: Disruption is moderate: significant portions of the work are cognitive and digital (researching venues, drafting communications, comparing bids, managing schedules, surveying attendees) where AI tools materially help, but the core work requires in-person relationship-building, on-site venue inspection, real-time problem-solving during live events, and physical presence that AI cannot replace. Elasticity is moderate because cheaper, faster planning could unlock more events at the lower end (smaller weddings, corporate gatherings), but demand for professional planners is constrained by budgets, the inherently social and high-touch nature of events, and the fact that major events are discrete, infrequent purchases. Because disruption stays at or below 6, the occupation is resilient—AI augments the administrative and research tasks but does not reshape the relationship-driven, physically present core of the role.

title: Metal and plastic machine workers
rationale: The core work is physical and hands-on: setting up machines, loading materials, swapping cutting tools, inspecting parts, and monitoring equipment on the factory floor. AI and automation (CNC, robotics) do reshape the industry, but the disruption here comes primarily from industrial machine automation rather than generative AI absorbing cognitive tasks; the manual setup, material handling, and inspection presence still requires human workers, keeping disruption low-to-moderate. Demand elasticity is low because output is driven by physical manufacturing orders that are capped by foreign competition and capital investment rather than unlocked by cheaper labor, so productivity gains translate into headcount reduction (BLS projects -7%). Because disruption is well below 7, this falls into the resilient category—AI touches the periphery and automation pressures employment, but it does not transform the fundamental physical nature of the core work.

title: Microbiologists
rationale: Microbiology involves substantial hands-on lab work — culturing organisms, running experiments, collecting field samples, operating physical equipment — that AI cannot perform, anchoring disruption to the moderate range. However, AI materially accelerates the cognitive portions: experimental design, genomic/sequence analysis, literature synthesis, report writing, and pattern recognition in microbial data, so the knowledge-work component is meaningfully affected. Demand has moderate elasticity because cheaper, faster analysis could expand research output in drug discovery, biofuels, and public health, but headcount growth is constrained by physical lab requirements and grant funding limits. Since core work remains heavily lab-bound and disruption stays at or below 6, the occupation is best classified as resilient.

title: Middle school teachers
rationale: The core work of middle school teaching is in-person classroom management, supervision of adolescents, emotional support, and real-time engagement—activities requiring sustained human presence that AI cannot replace. AI meaningfully assists peripheral tasks like lesson planning, grading, generating materials, and personalized practice content, which raises disruption to a moderate level, but the central job remains physically and socially anchored. Demand elasticity is low because student enrollment is fixed by demographics, class sizes and staffing are constrained by budgets and regulation, and cheaper AI tools do not increase the number of children needing teachers (the BLS projects a slight decline). Because disruption stays at or below 6, the occupation is classified as resilient: AI augments teacher productivity at the margins but does not reshape the core supervisory and relational work.

title: Military careers
rationale: Military careers span an enormous range of roles, but the core of the occupation centers on physical readiness, combat capability, security clearances, leadership under fire, and human presence in unpredictable real-world environments — tasks AI cannot replace. AI will materially change intelligence analysis, logistics, cyber, and administrative support roles, but the dominant mass of the force (combat, transportation, protective service, hands-on technical work) remains physical and human-dependent, yielding a moderate disruption score. Demand for military headcount is driven by geopolitical threat levels and policy/budget decisions rather than by productivity or cost efficiency, so it is highly inelastic to AI-driven gains. Because disruption stays at or below 6 and the work core is fundamentally physical and policy-driven, the occupation is resilient overall, with AI augmenting peripheral knowledge-work specialties rather than reshaping the core mission.

title: Mining and geological engineers
rationale: A significant portion of mining engineering work is digital and cognitive — mine design, geological analysis, technical report writing, and production monitoring — all of which AI can meaningfully assist. However, core duties require on-site presence, supervising mine construction, inspecting safety conditions, and field work in remote locations, which keeps disruption moderate rather than high. Demand is constrained by the physical limits of mineral extraction, regulatory and environmental approvals, and commodity market cycles, so productivity gains tend to reduce headcount rather than expand the workforce (BLS projects flat employment with automation offsetting growth). Because disruption falls at or below 6, the occupation is best classified as resilient — AI reshapes the analytical periphery but the physical, on-site, safety-critical core remains human-dependent.

title: Models
rationale: Modeling is physical posing, but its core output—images for advertising—is now directly in AI's path; generative AI can create photorealistic synthetic models and reuse/alter existing model images without new shoots, undermining the core economic value of the human model. Demand is largely inelastic because advertising image needs are bounded by the number of products and campaigns, and cheaper synthetic imagery substitutes for rather than expands human modeling work. With disruption high and elasticity low, productivity gains accrue to brands and AI tools rather than expanding human headcount, consistent with the BLS-projected decline driven explicitly by AI image reuse. This fits 'replace' (disruption >= 7, elasticity <= 4).

title: Music directors and composers
rationale: The composing portion of this work is highly disrupted—AI music generation tools can already produce arrangements, jingles, and background scores, directly threatening the commercial composition segment. However, the music director/conductor role is fundamentally a live, physical, interpersonal leadership task involving real-time human performance and ensemble coordination, which AI cannot replace, pulling the blended disruption score down to 6. On elasticity, cheaper music production could expand demand for low-cost commercial and background music, but the prestige live-performance segment (orchestras, opera, religious organizations comprising the majority of employment) is funding-constrained and culturally tied to human performers, limiting expansion to moderate. Because the core conducting and live-leadership work remains human-centric and disruption stays at 6, this occupation is resilient rather than facing wholesale restructuring.

title: Musicians and singers
rationale: While AI can generate music and synthetic vocals that may compete with recorded/session/background work, the core of this occupation—live performance, audience connection, stage presence, and the cultural authenticity of human artists—remains fundamentally physical and human, limiting disruption to a moderate level. Demand for live music has some room to expand with cheaper production tools that lower barriers for independent artists, but the live performance market is constrained by venue capacity, audience time, and the premium placed on human authenticity. Because disruption sits at or below 6, the occupation is classified as resilient: AI reshapes the recorded and production periphery (and may pressure session/background work) but does not transform the irreplaceable live-performance core.

title: Natural sciences managers
rationale: Much of the work involves knowledge tasks—reviewing research, drafting reports, analyzing data, and communicating findings—which AI tools can materially assist, pushing disruption toward moderate-high. However, the core of the role is leadership, team supervision, strategic decision-making, and interpersonal coordination requiring human judgment and accountability, which keeps disruption at 6 rather than higher. Elasticity is moderate because cheaper/faster research could expand R&D output and the number of projects requiring oversight, but management headcount is flexible and can be consolidated. Since disruption is at or below 6, the occupation falls into the resilient category: AI augments the analytical periphery but does not reshape the fundamentally human leadership core.

title: Network and computer systems administrators
rationale: The work is predominantly digital and cognitive — configuring systems, monitoring performance, automating tasks, diagnosing problems — all directly in AI's path, and much routine administration is already being automated and shifted to DevOps and Networks-as-a-Service models. Demand elasticity is low: organizations have a relatively fixed number of networks and systems to maintain, and cheaper administration does not cause businesses to consume dramatically more network infrastructure; productivity gains flow into headcount reduction rather than expanded output, consistent with the BLS-projected 4% decline. With disruption at 8 and elasticity at 4, this fits 'replace' — AI absorbs core routine work while demand fails to expand enough to preserve jobs.

title: News analysts, reporters, and journalists
rationale: Core tasks—researching, writing, editing, summarizing, and creating content across platforms—are predominantly language and cognitive work that AI tools already perform competently, driving a high disruption score, though in-person interviews, field reporting, and source relationships remain partly human. Demand elasticity is low because the industry's revenue base (advertising) is structurally declining and total appetite for original journalism is not strongly suppressed by production cost; cheaper content production tends to flood the market with low-value material rather than expand paid demand for professional reporters. With disruption >=7 and elasticity <=4, plus an already-declining BLS outlook, the occupation fits replace, as productivity gains and AI-generated content translate into headcount contraction rather than expanded output.

title: Nuclear engineers
rationale: Nuclear engineering involves substantial computational design, simulation, modeling, and analysis work that AI can meaningfully accelerate, but core responsibilities also require physical presence at plants, regulatory oversight, hands-on safety monitoring, and accountability that AI cannot assume, holding disruption at moderate. Demand has some upside given renewed interest in nuclear power and small modular reactors, but is heavily constrained by regulation, capital intensity, long construction timelines, and public/political factors, yielding moderate elasticity. Because disruption sits at 6 — below the high-disruption threshold — the occupation qualifies as resilient: AI augments design and analysis tasks but does not reshape the safety-critical, regulated, physically-anchored core of the work.

title: Nuclear medicine technologists
rationale: The core work is physical and hands-on: preparing and administering radioactive drugs, positioning and reassuring patients, operating large imaging equipment, and following strict radiation safety protocols requiring physical presence. AI may assist with image processing, dosing calculations, and record-keeping, but the radiopharmaceutical handling and patient interaction cannot be automated, keeping disruption low. Demand is relatively inelastic since the number of nuclear imaging procedures is driven by clinical need, physician referrals, and regulation rather than cost or speed, so cheaper AI assistance would not dramatically expand procedure volume. With disruption well below 7, this occupation is resilient — AI touches the periphery but does not reshape the core hands-on role.

title: Nuclear technicians
rationale: Disruption is moderate: while data analysis, radiation monitoring calculations, and reporting could be aided by AI, the core work requires hands-on physical presence in plants, onsite radiation measurement, equipment calibration/maintenance, and incident response in regulated, safety-critical environments that demand human oversight. Elasticity is low because demand for nuclear technicians is tied to the number of operating nuclear facilities, which is constrained by regulation, capital costs, and the shift to renewables—cheaper analysis won't trigger more plants or more monitoring activity. Since disruption is well below 7, the occupation is resilient: AI may streamline reporting and data interpretation but cannot replace the physical, regulated, safety-focused core of the job.

title: Nurse anesthetists, nurse midwives, and nurse practitioners
rationale: Disruption is moderate: while diagnostic reasoning, test interpretation, documentation, and care planning are cognitive tasks where AI provides meaningful decision support, the core work requires hands-on physical presence—administering anesthesia, delivering babies, performing exams, monitoring vitals, and the compassionate human interaction central to patient-centered care cannot be replaced by AI. Elasticity is high because healthcare demand is heavily suppressed by access and cost constraints, with an aging population, rising chronic disease, physician shortages, and expanding scope-of-practice laws all driving the projected 35% growth—cheaper, faster care unlocks substantial latent demand, especially in underserved areas. Because disruption falls at or below 6, the occupation is resilient: AI augments diagnostic and administrative portions but does not reshape the hands-on clinical core, and demand expansion strongly favors continued headcount growth.

title: Nursing assistants and orderlies
rationale: The core work—bathing, lifting, repositioning, feeding, and physically transporting patients—is hands-on, physical care requiring constant human presence, compassion, and dexterity that AI cannot perform. AI touches only peripheral tasks like recording vitals or documentation, leaving the daily job nearly unchanged. Demand is highly elastic given the aging population and chronic disease burden, and is currently suppressed by labor cost and shortages, so cheaper support would expand care coverage. Because disruption is very low (<=6), the occupation is resilient regardless of the high latent demand.

title: Occupational health and safety specialists and technicians
rationale: The disruption score is moderate because while data analysis, report writing, incident investigation trend-finding, and regulatory research can be substantially accelerated by AI, the core work requires physical presence: on-site inspections, hands-on testing of air quality and equipment, demonstrating safety gear, and walking factory floors, mines, and construction sites. Elasticity is moderate because regulatory mandates and employer safety priorities create durable, somewhat expandable demand—new technologies like robotics and emerging hazards like heat increase the need for inspections—but compliance requirements cap how much cheaper analysis would multiply total demand. Since disruption is at or below 6 and the work remains anchored to physical fieldwork and regulatory enforcement, the occupation is resilient: AI augments the documentation and analytical periphery without reshaping the inspection-and-compliance core.

title: Occupational therapists
rationale: The core work of occupational therapy is hands-on, physical, and deeply interpersonal—evaluating clients in person, demonstrating exercises, lifting/moving patients, and building rapport requiring compassion and patience. AI can assist with peripheral tasks like documentation, billing, treatment plan templates, and progress tracking, but cannot replace the manual, presence-based therapeutic interaction. Demand is moderately elastic given the aging population and unmet need, but it's driven by demographics and regulation rather than cost barriers AI would remove. With disruption well below 6, this occupation is resilient: AI touches the administrative periphery while the human-centered core remains intact.

title: Occupational therapy assistants and aides
rationale: The core work is hands-on physical therapy delivery—guiding clients through exercises, assisting with movement, lifting patients, and providing in-person therapeutic interaction—which AI cannot perform; only peripheral tasks like documentation, scheduling, and progress tracking can be assisted by AI. This yields a low disruption score since the essential tasks require human presence, dexterity, and compassion. Demand is moderately elastic given the aging population and the role's cost-reducing function relative to occupational therapists, though insurance reimbursement constraints cap expansion. Because disruption is well below the threshold, this occupation is resilient: AI streamlines administrative work but does not reshape the physical, relational core of the job.

title: Oil and gas workers
rationale: The core work is overwhelmingly physical: assembling, operating, maintaining, and repairing drilling equipment at remote outdoor sites, working at heights and in confined spaces. AI's relevance is mostly indirect through automated drilling, robotics, and remote monitoring that reduce headcount per rig, but the hands-on extraction tasks still require human crews present in the field. Demand is tied to commodity production volumes set by global energy markets and regulation rather than by the cost or speed of the labor itself, so productivity gains tend to translate into fewer workers rather than expanded output. With disruption well below the threshold, this occupation is resilient—AI touches the periphery and automation slowly thins crews, but it does not reshape the fundamentally physical core work.

title: Operations research analysts
rationale: The work is almost entirely digital and cognitive—data collection, statistical modeling, forecasting, optimization, and report writing—all directly in AI's path, with modern analytical software and ML tools already automating much of the modeling and data processing. Elasticity is high because analytical decision-support is currently cost- and expertise-constrained; cheaper, faster analysis would unlock latent demand as more organizations and more business processes (pricing, supply chains, scheduling) become worth optimizing. BLS projects 21% growth, reflecting that productivity gains expand rather than shrink the field. This fits augment: high disruption shifts the skill mix toward orchestrating AI tools and framing problems, while expanding demand absorbs the productivity gains and keeps headcount growing.

title: Opticians
rationale: Disruption is moderate because while administrative tasks (sales records, work orders, prescription interpretation, inventory) and even some frame/style recommendation could be AI-assisted, the core work involves physical measurement of customers' faces, hands-on fitting and adjustment of eyewear, and in-person customer service that requires real-world presence and dexterity. Demand elasticity is low because eyewear needs are driven by prescription rates and an aging population rather than by cost or speed—people don't buy dramatically more glasses if the fitting process becomes cheaper, and online retail represents substitution rather than market expansion. Since disruption falls at or below the moderate threshold, the occupation is resilient: AI touches the periphery (admin, recommendation tools) but cannot reshape the physically grounded fitting and dispensing core.

title: Optometrists
rationale: Disruption is moderate: AI strongly assists diagnostic portions (analyzing retinal images, detecting glaucoma/diabetic retinopathy, automated refraction) but core work requires in-person eye exams, hands-on procedures, prescribing, patient counseling, and legally mandated licensed presence. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper, faster screening could expand access and catch more vision problems in an aging, increasingly myopic population, but routine eye care demand is somewhat fixed per person and constrained by physical exam requirements.
