Since disruption stays at or below 6, the occupation is resilient—AI augments diagnostics and improves throughput but does not reshape the fundamentally physical, regulated, patient-facing core of the work.

title: Orthotists and prosthetists
rationale: The disruption score is moderate because while AI can enhance the design phase (CAD/CAM modeling, 3D scanning, automated fabrication), the core work requires hands-on patient assessment, physical measurement/molding, fitting, adjustment, and compassionate patient interaction that cannot be automated. AI tools materially assist the digital design portion but the occupation remains anchored in physical presence and dexterity. Elasticity is moderate-to-high since cheaper, faster device production could expand access to underserved patients and an aging, diabetic population drives growing demand. Because disruption stays at or below 6, the occupation is resilient—AI reshapes the design and fabrication workflow but does not displace the fundamentally hands-on, patient-centered core of the role.

title: Painters, construction and maintenance
rationale: Painting is almost entirely physical hands-on work involving surface preparation, climbing, brushing, rolling, and spraying in unpredictable real-world environments, with AI relevant only to peripheral tasks like estimating and color matching. Even if assistance tools made the cognitive portions faster, the core manual labor cannot be automated, so disruption is minimal. Demand is somewhat constrained by cost and DIY substitution, giving modest elasticity but no near-unlimited latent demand. With disruption far below the threshold, this occupation is clearly resilient to AI-driven change.

title: Painting and coating workers
rationale: Core work is overwhelmingly physical: surface preparation, machine setup, spray gun operation, bending into hard-to-reach areas, lifting heavy products, and visual quality inspection. AI is irrelevant to these manual tasks, though industrial robotics (a separate automation track) has long pressured manufacturing painting jobs—but that is mechanical automation, not AI cognition. Demand is fixed by physical output needs like cars and furniture that require painting; cheaper AI software wouldn't unlock dramatically more painted products. With disruption well below 6, this occupation is resilient to AI specifically, even as it faces slow growth from longstanding robotic automation.

title: Paralegals and legal assistants
rationale: Paralegal work is predominantly digital and language-based — legal research, document drafting, organizing files, and correspondence are all directly in AI's path and already meaningfully assisted by current legal AI tools, driving a high disruption score. Demand elasticity is low because legal services demand is constrained by structural factors: court capacity, regulatory limits, client willingness to pay, and the fact that cheaper paralegal support primarily reduces firm costs rather than dramatically expanding case volume. While some latent demand for legal services exists, it is capped by the same regulatory and procedural bottlenecks that limit lawyers. With disruption >=7 and elasticity <=4, productivity gains are likely absorbed as fewer workers per matter rather than expanded output, fitting the replace category, consistent with BLS's flat 0% growth projection citing AI efficiency gains.

title: Personal financial advisors
rationale: Disruption is high because core tasks—portfolio analysis, research, investment selection, financial planning, and reporting—are cognitive and digital, and robo-advisors plus AI assistants already automate substantial portions of the analytical work. However, the trust-building, interpersonal, and sales-driven relationship management remains a meaningful human anchor, capping disruption short of very high. Elasticity is moderate: an aging population, the shift from pensions to self-directed retirement accounts, and cheaper advice unlock more demand for financial planning, but social/regulatory constraints and the personal-relationship nature limit explosive growth. With disruption at 7 and elasticity at 6, the occupation survives but shifts toward client relationships, complex planning, and oversight of AI tools rather than routine analysis—fitting restructure.

title: Pest control workers
rationale: Core work is overwhelmingly physical and on-site: inspecting buildings, crawling into tight spaces, applying chemicals, setting traps, and sealing structures—none of which AI can perform. AI might assist peripherally with pest identification, scheduling, route optimization, or estimating, but these are minor relative to the hands-on labor. Demand is relatively fixed by actual infestation rates and is constrained by the need for licensed physical presence, so cheaper digital tools would not dramatically expand the volume of pest control jobs. With disruption well below 6, the occupation is clearly resilient.

title: Petroleum engineers
rationale: Much of petroleum engineering is data analysis, reservoir modeling, simulation, and design work — all highly susceptible to AI augmentation — but the role also requires significant on-site presence, oversight of drilling operations, troubleshooting physical equipment, and coordination with field crews that AI cannot replace, keeping disruption at a moderate 6. Demand elasticity is low because total oil and gas output is governed by commodity prices, reserves, regulatory constraints, and the energy transition rather than by the cost or speed of engineering analysis, so cheaper engineering would not meaningfully expand extraction volume. Because disruption stays at or below 6, the occupation is classified as resilient: AI reshapes the analytical periphery and boosts productivity, but the core blend of physical oversight and judgment-heavy field work remains human-dependent.

title: Pharmacists
rationale: Much of pharmacy's cognitive core—drug interaction checking, dosage verification, inventory management, and record-keeping—is highly amenable to AI automation, and dispensing is increasingly automated. However, significant portions of the role require physical presence (administering vaccinations, compounding), regulated human verification, and direct patient/clinician interaction that AI cannot fully replace, holding disruption to moderate. Demand is relatively inelastic since prescription volume is driven by medical need and regulation rather than cost or speed, limiting demand expansion from cheaper service. Because disruption stays at or below 6 (the core dispensing function is legally and physically anchored to licensed humans), the occupation is best classified as resilient—AI reshapes workflows and shifts pharmacists toward clinical/patient-care roles without gutting the profession.

title: Pharmacy technicians
rationale: The work mixes physical, hands-on tasks (counting, measuring, packaging, compounding, IV preparation, inventory handling) with cognitive and data tasks (entering prescriptions, processing insurance, verifying orders) — AI and automated dispensing systems already streamline the digital portions but the core requires physical presence and regulated human verification, placing disruption in the moderate range. Demand is expanding due to aging demographics and chronic disease prevalence, and pharmacy techs are absorbing tasks shifted from pharmacists, but prescription volume isn't dramatically suppressed by cost or speed, keeping elasticity moderate. Because disruption stays at or below 6, the occupation is resilient: AI automates peripheral and routine tasks but does not reshape the hands-on, regulated, customer-facing core, and projected employment continues to grow.

title: Phlebotomists
rationale: Phlebotomy is fundamentally a hands-on physical task requiring dexterity, patient interaction, and real-world presence to draw blood, label samples, and manage anxious patients—AI touches only peripheral tasks like data entry and sample tracking. Demand is driven by medical necessity and an aging population rather than cost suppression, so cheaper administrative processes wouldn't dramatically increase the number of blood draws ordered. With disruption well below the threshold, the occupation is resilient: AI may streamline record-keeping but cannot replace the core physical and interpersonal work.

title: Photographers
rationale: The core work of photography requires physical presence to capture real subjects, scenes, and events — a portrait, wedding, news event, or product shoot demands a human behind the camera in the real world, which AI cannot replicate. However, the postproduction, editing, composition assistance, and notably generative image creation are squarely in AI's path, and AI-generated imagery plus stock photo services already pressure commercial and stock-oriented segments. On elasticity, demand for professional capture services is fairly fixed by social needs (weddings, portraits, news) and is being eroded rather than expanded by cheaper alternatives like smartphones and AI generation, so productivity gains do not unlock large latent demand. Because the disruption to the core physical capture work stays at or below 6 and AI mostly displaces peripheral or generative substitutes rather than reshaping the act of professional photography, the occupation is best classified as resilient with slow growth.

title: Physical therapist assistants and aides
rationale: The core work is intensely physical and hands-on: manual therapy, guiding exercises, moving and lifting patients, and providing compassionate in-person care. AI can only touch peripheral tasks like scheduling, documentation, and insurance forms, leaving the vast majority of daily duties untouched. Demand is highly elastic given an aging population and chronic-disease prevalence, with physical therapy currently constrained by cost and provider availability, so cheaper administrative overhead could free up more direct care time. Because disruption is far below the threshold of 7, the occupation is resilient regardless of strong demand growth.

title: Physical therapists
rationale: The core work of physical therapy is hands-on, physical, and requires in-person presence — manual therapy, demonstrating exercises, physically assisting and moving patients — which AI cannot perform. AI touches only peripheral tasks like documentation, progress tracking, treatment plan suggestions, and remote monitoring, leaving the central duties intact. Demand is meaningfully elastic given aging demographics, growing chronic conditions, and a shift toward nonopioid pain management, so cheaper administrative support would free therapists for more patient care. With disruption well below the threshold, this occupation is resilient regardless of elasticity.

title: Physician assistants
rationale: PAs combine substantial cognitive/diagnostic work (history-taking, interpreting tests, treatment planning) that AI can meaningfully assist with, alongside hands-on physical care like examinations, suturing, setting bones, and surgical assistance that requires human presence — placing disruption in the moderate range. Demand is highly elastic: aging populations, chronic disease growth, provider shortages, and underserved rural areas mean cheaper/faster care unlocks large latent demand, and PAs are specifically valued because they expand provider capacity. Despite high elasticity, the core work is only moderately disrupted (physical presence, licensure, and supervised clinical judgment dominate), so the occupation is resilient — AI augments documentation and decision support but does not reshape the hands-on, patient-facing core.

title: Physicians and surgeons
rationale: Physician work blends substantial cognitive/diagnostic tasks (history-taking, image interpretation, treatment planning, documentation) that AI already meaningfully assists with—and some specialties like radiology and pathology are heavily image/data-based—but the core of most physician work requires physical examination, hands-on procedures, surgery, real-time clinical judgment under liability, and human compassion, keeping disruption moderate rather than high. Demand elasticity is high because healthcare need is enormous and currently rationed by physician scarcity, cost, and access; cheaper, faster diagnostics and AI-augmented productivity would unlock large amounts of latent demand, especially with an aging population and chronic-disease burden. Because aggregate disruption stays at or below the moderate threshold (AI augments the knowledge portions but cannot replace the licensed, physical, judgment-laden core), the net effect is resilient—AI reshapes workflows and tools without contracting headcount.

title: Physicists and astronomers
rationale: Much of physics and astronomy work is heavily computational and cognitive—data analysis, modeling, simulation, software development, and writing papers and proposals—all of which AI tools can already materially accelerate, driving a high disruption score. However, core elements like designing physical experiments, operating particle accelerators and telescopes, and generating genuinely novel theoretical insight remain human-anchored, keeping disruption below the very-high tier. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper, faster analysis could unlock more research output and broaden the range of problems tackled, but the field is structurally constrained by federal funding budgets that cap headcount growth regardless of productivity gains. With high disruption and moderate elasticity, the occupation fits restructure—skill sets shift toward AI-augmented modeling and analysis, and adaptable researchers thrive while routine computational roles compress.

title: Plumbers, pipefitters, and steamfitters
rationale: The core work is physical and hands-on: installing pipes, fixing leaks, soldering, working in tight spaces, and troubleshooting systems in unpredictable real-world environments — none of which AI can perform. AI touches only peripheral tasks like cost estimation, blueprint/BIM design assistance, and scheduling. Demand is driven by physical infrastructure needs, building codes, and emergency repairs, which are not strongly suppressed by cost or speed, so productivity gains in admin tasks won't dramatically expand the work. With disruption well below 6, this occupation is firmly resilient regardless of elasticity.

title: Podiatrists
rationale: Podiatry is fundamentally hands-on physical medicine—diagnosing, treating, and surgically operating on feet, ankles, and lower legs—requiring in-person examination and manual procedures that AI cannot perform. AI may assist with diagnostic imaging interpretation, documentation, and treatment-planning peripherally, but the core surgical and physical-treatment tasks remain firmly human. Demand is somewhat constrained by an aging population needing more care but capped by competition from other physicians and licensing/regulatory structure. With disruption well below 6, this occupation is resilient: AI touches administrative and diagnostic edges but does not reshape the physical, patient-facing core.

title: Police and detectives
rationale: Core police work is physical and presence-based — patrolling, responding to emergencies, apprehending suspects, conducting interviews, and managing volatile real-world situations that AI cannot perform. AI does meaningfully assist peripheral knowledge tasks like report writing, database searches, evidence analysis, predictive policing, and surveillance, which raises disruption to moderate, but the irreplaceable physical and judgment-based duties keep it from going higher. Elasticity is low because demand for policing is driven by public safety needs and constrained by government budgets rather than the cost or speed of service, so productivity gains do not unlock dramatically more demand. With disruption at 4, the occupation is resilient: AI augments documentation and investigation but does not reshape the fundamentally human, physical core of the work.

title: Political scientists
rationale: The core work — researching political systems, analyzing public opinion data, testing theories, forecasting trends, and writing reports — is almost entirely cognitive, language-based, and data-driven, placing it squarely in AI's path; modern LLMs and analytics tools already perform literature synthesis, survey analysis, and trend forecasting effectively. Demand is structurally constrained: 67% of these jobs sit in the federal government and depend heavily on budget allocations rather than market price, so cheaper analysis does not unlock proportionally more consumption, and BLS already projects a 3% decline. The small, inelastic, government-dependent demand combined with high task automatability means productivity gains translate to fewer needed analysts rather than expanded output, fitting the replace category.

title: Postal service workers
rationale: The core work is overwhelmingly physical—carriers deliver mail on foot and by vehicle (64% of the workforce), and sorters load/unload trucks and operate machinery—tasks requiring real-world presence that AI cannot perform, though automated sorting (already long-established) does erode the processing roles. Demand is inelastic: physical mail volume is structurally declining due to digital communications, and cheaper/faster sorting does not create more letters to deliver; productivity gains let carriers absorb larger routes rather than expanding total demand. Because disruption sits well below the 7 threshold and is concentrated in peripheral automation rather than reshaping the physical delivery core, this occupation is resilient to AI even as it slowly contracts for unrelated structural reasons.

title: Postsecondary education administrators
rationale: The work mixes substantial administrative/data tasks (records management, application processing, scheduling, data analysis) that AI can automate or accelerate with deeply human leadership, interpersonal, advising, and policy functions (deans, provosts, student affairs) that resist automation. This places disruption at a moderate level since AI heavily affects registrar and admissions back-office work but not the relationship-driven and governance core. Elasticity is low because demand is structurally tied to student enrollment and institutional budgets, with deans/provost roles capped at a fixed number per institution—cheaper administration won't generate dramatically more administrators. Because disruption stays at or below 6, the occupation is resilient: AI streamlines tasks but does not reshape the fundamental human-centered nature of the role.

title: Postsecondary teachers
rationale: Core tasks—lecturing, grading, research, curriculum design, advising—are heavily cognitive and language-based, and AI already materially assists with content generation, grading support, and research, pushing disruption toward high. However, the occupation's value rests substantially on in-person instruction, mentorship, accreditation requirements, credentialing of students, and the social/institutional role of universities, which anchor the human core and keep disruption at a moderate 6. Demand has moderate elasticity: enrollment growth (especially health specialties and nursing) and lifelong learning could expand demand, but state budget constraints, fixed degree structures, and institutional gatekeeping cap expansion. Because disruption sits at 6 (not >=7), the occupation falls into resilient—AI reshapes how teaching and research are done at the periphery but does not displace the core human-presence and credentialing functions.

title: Power plant operators, distributors, and dispatchers
rationale: The work is a mix of control-room monitoring (digital, increasingly automated via smart-grid and modernized control systems) and physical presence, equipment rounds, emergency response, and regulatory/safety oversight that requires human judgment and licensed operators physically on site. AI and automation materially assist monitoring and routine tasks like power rerouting, but core responsibilities for safety-critical operation, NRC-licensed control, and unpredictable emergency response keep humans essential, placing disruption at a moderate 5. Demand is highly inelastic since electricity output is governed by physical grid capacity and consumption, not by how cheap operator labor becomes—productivity gains translate to fewer workers (the BLS projects -10%) rather than expanded output. Because disruption is at or below 6, the occupation is resilient: AI reshapes peripheral tasks and trims headcount through efficiency, but does not fundamentally replace the core safety-critical operating role.

title: Preschool and childcare center directors
rationale: The core work involves in-person supervision of staff and children, building relationships with parents, managing facilities, and ensuring regulatory compliance — all requiring physical presence and human judgment that AI cannot replace. AI can assist with peripheral tasks like budgeting, scheduling, record-keeping, and parent communications, but these are a minority of daily responsibilities. Demand is inelastic and constrained by demographics (low birth rates), the high cost of childcare, and regulatory caps on staff-to-child ratios, so productivity gains won't dramatically expand the number of directors needed. With disruption well below 6, this occupation is resilient: AI touches administrative edges but leaves the fundamentally human, on-site management role intact.

title: Preschool teachers
rationale: The core work—physically caring for, supervising, and emotionally nurturing children under five through play, hands-on activities, and constant in-person supervision—is fundamentally physical and interpersonal, leaving AI to touch only peripheral tasks like lesson planning or progress documentation. Demand is structurally constrained by child-to-teacher ratio regulations, parental preference for human caregivers, and the fixed number of young children, so productivity gains in admin tasks cannot meaningfully reduce staffing needs. Because disruption is very low and the human caregiving requirement cannot be automated, this occupation is resilient regardless of elasticity.

title: Private detectives and investigators
rationale: A significant portion of the work — searching online and public records, analyzing social networks, court records, and writing reports — is digital cognitive work that AI tools materially accelerate, pulling the disruption score upward. However, core tasks like physical surveillance, undercover store detection, in-person interviews, and gathering legally admissible evidence require human presence and judgment that AI cannot replace, capping disruption at moderate. Demand could expand modestly as cheaper background checks and skip-tracing unlock more cases, but social mistrust, regulatory limits, and the irreducibly physical nature of much of the work bound elasticity to moderate. Because disruption is at or below 6, the occupation is classified as resilient — AI reshapes the research portion but leaves the physical, interpersonal, and legal core intact.

title: Probation officers and correctional treatment specialists
rationale: The core work involves in-person supervision, home/employment visits, drug testing, building relationships with hostile or vulnerable clients, court testimony, and judgment-heavy risk assessment that requires unpredictable real-world presence and physical safety considerations. AI can meaningfully assist the documentation, report-writing, risk-scoring, and case-file management portions, but the central tasks remain inherently human and field-based, keeping disruption moderate. Demand is structurally fixed by criminal justice caseloads and government corrections funding, not by cost or speed, so productivity gains would not expand the client population. Because disruption stays at or below 6, the occupation is resilient—AI augments the administrative periphery without reshaping the supervisory and counseling core.

title: Producers and directors
rationale: Disruption is moderate-to-high: AI tools increasingly assist with scriptwriting, editing, scheduling, budgeting, visual effects, and even generative content production, but the core creative and leadership role of producers and directors — interpreting a vision, coordinating large human teams, making nuanced casting and artistic decisions, and managing live or on-location production — remains fundamentally human and not fully digital. Elasticity is high because cheaper, faster production tools dramatically lower barriers to content creation, expanding the total volume of video, streaming, and advertising output that needs creative oversight. However, because the disruption score sits at 6 (below the 7 threshold), AI reshapes the peripheral and technical tasks rather than the irreducible human core of orchestrating and creatively directing productions, making this occupation resilient. The faster-than-average projected job growth supports continued demand for these workers even as their toolkits evolve.

title: Project management specialists
rationale: The core work — planning, scheduling, budgeting, documentation, status tracking, and reporting — is heavily digital and cognitive, and AI tools already automate much of the documentation, plan generation, risk modeling, and progress monitoring, driving a high disruption score. However, the interpersonal coordination, stakeholder trust-building, and accountability for outcomes remain hard to automate, so AI augments rather than replaces the human. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper, faster project coordination lets organizations run more projects and apply formal management to smaller efforts, but demand is constrained by the number of actual projects organizations undertake. With disruption >=7 and elasticity at 5, the occupation survives but shifts toward higher-level orchestration and judgment skills while routine tracking work is absorbed by AI, fitting restructure.

title: Property appraisers and assessors
rationale: The core analytical work—comparing comparables, analyzing data, producing valuation reports, and mass appraisal via computer-assisted systems—is heavily data-driven and squarely in AI's path, with automated valuation models (AVMs) already widely used; the main human-bound elements are site visits and photography, keeping disruption from being maximal. Demand for appraisals is structurally fixed: tied to real estate transactions, tax assessment cycles, and regulatory mandates, so cheaper/faster appraisals do not unlock more transactions—people don't buy more homes or get more tax assessments because valuation is cheap. With high disruption and low, regulation-capped elasticity, productivity gains translate to fewer workers per task rather than expanded output, fitting the replace category, with licensing requirements being the main brake on headcount contraction.

title: Property, real estate, and community association managers
rationale: Disruption is moderate: significant portions of the work—financial reporting, budgeting, record-keeping, posting vacancies, scheduling maintenance, tenant communications—are digital and increasingly automated by AI and property management software. However, the core role requires physical presence (property inspections, showing units, on-site emergency response) and human interpersonal mediation (dispute resolution, board relations, tenant complaints) that AI cannot replace. Elasticity is low-to-moderate: demand is structurally tied to the number of managed properties and residents, which grows slowly with the housing stock rather than expanding because management got cheaper—people don't acquire more buildings simply because oversight is faster. Since disruption falls at or below 6, the occupation is resilient: AI automates the administrative periphery while the physical and relational core remains human-dependent, consistent with the modest 4% projected growth.

title: Psychiatric technicians and aides
rationale: The core work is overwhelmingly physical and interpersonal: monitoring patients, assisting with daily living activities like bathing and eating, restraining violent patients, and providing hands-on therapeutic and recreational care. These tasks require constant human presence, physical stamina, compassion, and real-time judgment that AI cannot replace; AI might assist only peripherally with documentation or vital-sign monitoring. Demand is structurally expanding due to rising rates of mental illness and substance use disorders, though it is constrained by funding and facility capacity rather than cost-per-task. Because disruption is very low, the occupation is resilient regardless of elasticity — AI touches only the edges of this hands-on patient care role.

title: Psychologists
rationale: The work has significant cognitive and language-based components (assessment, research, report writing, treatment planning) where AI can assist, but the core of clinical and counseling psychology relies on human rapport, empathy, trust, observational nuance, and the therapeutic relationship that AI cannot replicate or legally substitute for licensed practice. Demand elasticity is high because mental health services are heavily cost- and access-constrained, and cheaper AI-augmented tools could expand reach to underserved populations, increasing total demand for human psychologists who supervise, validate, and provide irreplaceable in-person care. Because disruption remains at or below 6 — AI touches documentation, screening, and research support but does not reshape the relational and diagnostic core — the occupation is best classified as resilient, with productivity tools augmenting rather than replacing practitioners.

title: Public relations and fundraising managers
rationale: Much of the work — drafting press releases, writing speeches, content creation, monitoring social/media trends, and donor research — is language and cognitive work directly in AI's path, which pushes disruption up. However, the core of this role is managerial: relationship-building, in-person donor meetings, crisis judgment, leadership of teams, and high-stakes reputational decisions that require human accountability and trust, capping disruption at a moderate 6. Elasticity is moderate because cheaper content and outreach could expand campaign activity and let more organizations afford sophisticated PR/fundraising, but the relationship-driven and reputation-stakes nature limits unlimited expansion. Since disruption is at or below 6, the occupation is resilient: AI reshapes the production tasks beneath the manager while the supervisory, strategic, and interpersonal core remains human.

title: Public relations specialists
rationale: Core tasks—writing press releases, drafting speeches, monitoring social media, adapting content for multiple channels—are predominantly language and digital work directly in AI's path, driving a high disruption score; generative AI already materially accelerates content creation and sentiment analysis. Demand is moderately elastic: cheaper content production lets more organizations and segments invest in communications and crisis response, but PR ultimately rests on human relationships, media contacts, judgment on sensitive issues, and accountable spokesmanship that cap unlimited expansion. The work survives but shifts toward strategy, relationship management, and AI-augmented content oversight rather than manual drafting, fitting restructure as disruption is high and elasticity sits in the moderate band.

title: Public safety telecommunicators
rationale: The work is highly cognitive and language-based — answering calls, classifying emergencies, logging data, and dispatching — which AI can increasingly assist with (call triage, transcription, location detection, suggested protocols), but the core requires real-time human judgment, empathy under crisis, and high-stakes accountability that current AI cannot fully assume, capping disruption at moderate-to-high. Demand is inelastic: emergency call volume is fixed by population and incident rates, not by the cost or speed of handling each call, so cheaper processing does not generate dramatically more emergencies. Because disruption stays at or below 6 and the work is anchored by life-safety responsibility, the occupation is resilient — AI augments triage and documentation while humans remain firmly in the loop.

title: Purchasing managers, buyers, and purchasing agents
rationale: The work is predominantly cognitive and language/data-based — analyzing price proposals, comparing suppliers, reviewing records, monitoring inventory, and drafting/managing contracts — all of which AI procurement tools already materially automate, though negotiation and supplier relationship management retain a human component. Demand is structurally inelastic: an organization buys what it needs to operate or resell, and making procurement 10x cheaper doesn't cause companies to procure dramatically more goods; productivity gains accrue to fewer agents handling more transactions, with consolidation pressures (cooperative purchasing agreements, centralized e-procurement) further capping headcount. BLS itself notes automation and AI may limit growth. With disruption at 7 and elasticity at 3, this fits replace — core analytical and transactional tasks are absorbed by AI without offsetting demand expansion, leading to headcount contraction relative to output.

title: Quality control inspectors
rationale: Disruption is moderate: while AI-powered machine vision and automated inspection systems are increasingly replacing visual inspection tasks, much of the work still requires physical presence—handling parts, using calipers and gauges, lifting heavy materials, and conducting test runs in noisy plant environments. Elasticity is low because the volume of products needing inspection is tied to manufacturing output, which is fairly fixed; cheaper inspection does not unlock dramatically more demand for inspection itself. With disruption at 5 (below the 7 threshold), the occupation qualifies as resilient—AI automates portions of inspection but does not reshape the physically grounded core work, consistent with the flat 0% projected employment change.

title: Radiation therapists
rationale: The core work is hands-on: positioning patients, operating linear accelerators, lifting/turning patients, monitoring for reactions, and providing compassionate care over weeks of treatment—all requiring physical presence and human interaction that AI cannot replace. AI does meaningfully assist the planning and dosimetry portions (treatment planning, dose calculation, image analysis), but those are largely separate roles (dosimetrists, physicists), leaving the therapist's daily tasks only moderately affected. Demand is inelastic—patients receive a clinically determined course of radiation, and cheaper/faster processing doesn't generate more cancer needing treatment; indeed more efficient techniques reduce visits. Because disruption stays at or below 6, the occupation is resilient: AI touches the planning periphery but does not reshape the therapist's hands-on, patient-facing core.

title: Radiologic and MRI technologists
rationale: The core work involves hands-on patient positioning, equipment operation, patient preparation (injecting contrast, shielding), and physical presence with patients who may be in pain or injured—all tasks that require human physical presence and cannot be automated by AI. AI primarily affects the image interpretation side (radiologists), not the image acquisition performed by technologists, though AI may assist with workflow optimization and image quality checks at the periphery. Demand is moderately elastic given an aging population and rising chronic disease driving more imaging needs, but procedures still require expensive equipment and physical scan time per patient, capping growth. Because disruption to the core work is low (3), the occupation is resilient—AI touches administrative and quality-assurance edges but does not reshape the fundamentally physical, patient-facing nature of the job.

title: Railroad workers
rationale: Core tasks are overwhelmingly physical and require real-world presence: operating locomotive controls, coupling cars, monitoring tracks for obstructions, inspecting equipment, and managing crews in rail yards. While some automation (remote-controlled yard locomotives, automated signaling) and the prospect of autonomous trains exist, heavy regulation by the FRA, safety requirements, union agreements, and the physical complexity of rail operations sharply limit AI's reach into the core work. Demand is structurally constrained by fixed infrastructure and freight/passenger volumes that grow slowly, so productivity gains would not unlock large latent demand. With disruption well below the threshold, the occupation is resilient—AI touches peripheral coordination and monitoring but does not reshape the fundamentally hands-on, regulated nature of the work.

title: Real estate brokers and sales agents
rationale: Much of the work involves digital and cognitive tasks AI can assist (market analysis, pricing, listing generation, document preparation, lead generation), but the core value is relationship-driven: in-person property showings, negotiation, trust, and local knowledge keep this work anchored in human presence. AI tools materially augment the administrative and analytical portions but do not replace the high-stakes, relationship-based transaction the client is actually paying for. Demand is structurally inelastic because the volume of real estate transactions is capped by housing supply, household formation, and economic cycles rather than by the cost or speed of agent services; cheaper agents do not meaningfully increase the number of homes bought and sold. With disruption at or below 6 and the core work resistant to automation, this occupation is best classified as resilient.

title: Receptionists
rationale: The core tasks—answering phones, scheduling appointments, entering data, handling correspondence—are largely digital and language-based, exactly what AI scheduling systems, chatbots, and virtual receptionist tools already handle, driving high disruption. However, the in-person greeting, security, and physical visitor-handling functions provide partial insulation, keeping disruption just at 7. Demand is highly inelastic: an organization needs roughly one front desk regardless of how cheap automation becomes, so productivity gains convert to fewer positions rather than more reception services. High disruption combined with very low elasticity points to headcount contraction, consistent with the flat-to-declining BLS outlook and ongoing automation of administrative functions.

title: Recreation workers
rationale: Recreation work is fundamentally physical, in-person, and interpersonal—leading group activities, instructing participants, administering first aid, and motivating people in real-world settings that AI cannot perform. AI might touch only peripheral admin tasks like creating newsletters, calendars, or scheduling, leaving the core hands-on, presence-based work untouched. Demand is structurally tied to facility budgets, seniors needing care, and youth programs, so cheaper admin tools won't dramatically expand headcount but neither will they cause contraction. With disruption well below the 7 threshold, this occupation is clearly resilient.

title: Recreational therapists
rationale: The core work is hands-on, physically present therapeutic engagement—leading sports, games, arts, aquatics, and community outings while motivating and physically assisting patients—which AI cannot perform. AI can assist only with peripheral tasks like documentation, treatment-plan drafting, and progress tracking, leaving the human-delivered core essentially intact. Demand is structurally constrained by healthcare funding, certification requirements, and the inherently in-person nature of the service, so cheaper administrative support would not dramatically expand headcount. With disruption well below 6, the occupation is resilient regardless of elasticity.

title: Registered nurses
rationale: Nursing involves substantial physical, hands-on patient care—lifting patients, administering treatments, monitoring equipment, providing emotional support—that AI cannot replace, though AI does meaningfully assist documentation, diagnostics, care planning, and patient education, placing disruption at moderate. Demand is structurally elastic given aging demographics, chronic disease prevalence, and persistent workforce shortages, so productivity gains would be absorbed by expanded care rather than headcount cuts. Because the core work remains anchored in human presence and physical caregiving with disruption at 4, the occupation is resilient; AI augments peripheral cognitive tasks but does not reshape the fundamental role.

title: Rehabilitation counselors
rationale: The core work involves empathetic counseling, building trust, in-person assessment, advocacy, and physical resource coordination (e.g., locating wheelchairs)—all requiring human presence, compassion, and relationship-building that AI cannot replicate. AI can assist peripherally with documentation, resource matching, plan drafting, and progress tracking, but the central interpersonal counseling tasks remain human-driven, yielding a moderate disruption score. Demand is moderately elastic since cheaper administrative support could free counselors to serve more clients, but the work is heavily constrained by government budgets, regulatory licensure, and the fundamentally human caseload nature. With disruption at or below 6, the occupation is resilient: AI touches administrative edges but does not reshape the empathetic, presence-based core.

title: Respiratory therapists
rationale: Respiratory therapists perform hands-on physical work—administering treatments, operating ventilators, chest physiotherapy, drawing blood samples, and providing bedside patient care—that requires real-world physical presence and cannot be automated by AI. AI may assist peripherally with diagnostic test interpretation, monitoring data, and documentation, but the core therapeutic and patient-interaction tasks remain human-dependent. Demand is driven by aging demographics and respiratory disease prevalence rather than cost barriers, so productivity gains wouldn't dramatically expand consumption. With disruption well below 6, this occupation is resilient: AI touches the periphery (charting, analytics) but does not reshape the fundamentally physical, in-person nature of the work.

title: Retail sales workers
rationale: The core work is in-person customer interaction, physical product demonstration, stocking, and processing payments — tasks requiring real-world presence that AI cannot directly perform. AI affects the periphery (inventory systems, product recommendations, e-commerce competition that erodes foot traffic) but does not reshape the face-to-face selling core. Demand is also inelastic: cheaper retail labor does not unlock dramatically more in-store shopping, and the larger threat is e-commerce shifting volume away from physical stores rather than productivity-driven expansion. With disruption at or below 6, the occupation is resilient — AI touches the edges but the human-presence core remains intact, even if total headcount stays flat due to broader retail shifts.

title: Roofers
rationale: Roofing is almost entirely physical, hands-on work performed outdoors at heights, involving climbing, lifting, cutting, and installing materials in unpredictable real-world conditions—tasks AI cannot perform. AI is irrelevant to the core work, touching only peripheral functions like estimating or material calculations. Demand is structurally tied to building stock and weather-driven repair needs and is not heavily suppressed by labor cost in a way that would explode with cheaper output. With disruption far below the threshold, this occupation is clearly resilient regardless of elasticity.

title: Sales engineers
rationale: Much of a sales engineer's work involves digital and cognitive tasks—preparing technical presentations, analyzing product fit, generating proposals, and providing troubleshooting support—all of which AI tools can meaningfully accelerate. However, the core of the role relies on relationship-building, trust, persuasion, in-person customer engagement, and bespoke needs assessment that resist automation, keeping disruption moderate rather than high. On elasticity, cheaper and faster technical sales support could expand the number of products and customers covered, but headcount is structurally tied to deal volume and human relationship management, capping expansion at moderate levels. Because disruption stays at 6 (AI augments the knowledge-work portions but does not reshape the human-centered core), the occupation is best classified as resilient.

title: Sales managers
rationale: Sales managers perform significant data analysis, forecasting, and CRM work that AI tools already materially enhance, but the core of the role—leadership, motivating teams, building relationships, negotiating, and strategic judgment—relies on human interpersonal skills that AI cannot replace. This keeps disruption at the high end of moderate rather than fully high. Demand elasticity is moderate since cheaper sales analytics could let more organizations optimize sales strategy, but the management headcount is tied to team size and organizational structure rather than output volume. Because disruption stays at 6 (the periphery is automated but the leadership core remains human-centric), the occupation is resilient.

title: School and career counselors and advisors
rationale: The disruption score is moderate because while assessments, data analysis, college/career information lookup, and résumé/interview prep are clearly AI-augmentable, the core of the job—building trusting relationships, providing emotional support, handling sensitive student issues like abuse/neglect, and navigating school systems with parents and teachers—requires human presence, compassion, and judgment that AI cannot replicate. The elasticity is moderate because cheaper guidance could expand access (more underserved students get personalized career/college advice), but school counselor headcount is largely determined by enrollment, budgets, and state mandates rather than productivity-driven demand. Because disruption stays at or below 6, the occupation is resilient: AI tools will handle informational and administrative tasks, freeing counselors to focus on the interpersonal and developmental work that defines the role.

title: Secretaries and administrative assistants
rationale: Core tasks—document preparation, scheduling, email/memo writing, database management, transcription, and basic bookkeeping—are overwhelmingly digital and language-based, placing them directly in AI's path; modern tools already let managers and staff self-serve these functions, which BLS itself cites as a factor flattening employment. Demand is inelastic: organizations need a roughly fixed amount of administrative coordination, and cheaper/faster document handling does not cause businesses to consume dramatically more secretarial support—productivity gains translate into fewer support staff per manager rather than expanded output. With high disruption (8) and low elasticity (2), the occupation fits 'replace,' consistent with the flat-to-declining projections in most subcategories, with only medical secretaries partially insulated by healthcare-sector growth and physical/patient-facing tasks.

title: Securities, commodities, and financial services sales agents
rationale: The core work — market analysis, trade execution, securities valuation, portfolio recommendations, and financial modeling — is almost entirely digital, cognitive, and quantitative, putting it directly in AI's path; algorithmic trading and robo-advisors have already displaced large portions of trading and simple brokerage work. Demand elasticity is low because the total volume of trades, IPOs, M&A deals, and assets under management is bounded by macroeconomic activity and heavy regulation rather than by the cost of advice, so cheaper execution does not meaningfully multiply transaction volume. The relationship-driven, high-touch sales and client-trust segment provides some buffer, but the bulk of analytical and transactional tasks face automation without offsetting demand growth, yielding net headcount pressure consistent with replace (disruption >=7, elasticity <=4).

title: Security guards and gambling surveillance officers
rationale: The core work is physical and presence-based — patrolling, responding to emergencies, deterring crime, controlling access, and deescalating confrontations — which AI cannot replace, though the surveillance-monitoring portion (especially for gambling officers) is squarely in AI's path via cameras integrated with anomaly detection. This yields moderate disruption: AI augments the watching/monitoring tasks but the physical guarding and human response functions remain essential. Demand is largely inelastic and tied to fixed physical sites, crime concerns, and regulatory presence requirements; cheaper surveillance does not dramatically multiply the number of locations needing on-site guards. Because disruption stays at or below the moderate threshold and the occupation's physical core is untouched, it fits 'resilient.'

title: Semiconductor processing technicians
rationale: The core work is physical and presence-dependent: operating cleanroom equipment, handling wafers, performing hands-on quality control, and adjusting machinery in a sterile environment. AI and automation already permeate semiconductor fabs (robotics, automated inspection, process monitoring), but technicians remain essential for supervising automated systems, troubleshooting, and dexterity-intensive tasks that cannot be fully remote or digital, so disruption is moderate. Demand for semiconductors is strongly expanding due to broad device proliferation and US reshoring incentives, so productivity gains are likely absorbed by more fabs and output rather than headcount cuts, giving moderate-to-high elasticity. Because disruption stays at or below 6, the occupation is resilient—AI augments inspection and process control but does not reshape the hands-on core.

title: Set and exhibit designers
rationale: The design and conceptualization portion is heavily digital—CAD work, drawing, rendering, script analysis, and visualization are all directly in AI's path, and generative AI tools already produce concept art and 3D mockups, driving a high disruption score. However, the core work still requires real-world physical installation, on-site oversight, collaboration with directors/curators, and tactile spatial judgment that AI cannot replace, which keeps disruption from going higher. Elasticity is moderate because cheaper, faster design could unlock more exhibits, productions, and trade-show concepts, but total demand is structurally capped by physical venues, production budgets, and the limited number of films, shows, and museums. With disruption at 7 and elasticity at 6, the occupation fits restructure: surviving designers must shift toward AI-augmented ideation and physical execution while routine drafting roles shrink.

title: Sheet metal workers
rationale: The core work is physical fabrication and installation — measuring, cutting, bending, welding, climbing, and maneuvering heavy sheet metal in construction sites and shops — tasks that require hands-on dexterity and unpredictable real-world presence that AI cannot perform. AI and automation (CADD, CNC machines) touch only the design and programming portions, and prefabrication/automation pressures are already reflected in the slow 2% growth projection. Demand is structurally tied to construction and HVAC installation activity, which won't dramatically expand simply because design becomes cheaper, since physical installation cost dominates. With disruption well below 6, the occupation is resilient: AI affects the periphery but does not reshape the manual core of the work.

title: Skincare specialists
rationale: Skincare specialists perform almost entirely hands-on physical work—applying treatments, waxing, facials, massages, and hair removal directly to clients' skin—which AI cannot perform. AI touches only peripheral tasks like product recommendation, scheduling, or skin analysis tools, leaving the core service untouched. Demand could moderately expand with cheaper, faster booking and personalized skincare diagnostics, but the labor-intensive treatments themselves cap any productivity-driven volume growth. Because disruption is minimal, this occupation is resilient regardless of elasticity.

title: Small engine mechanics
rationale: The core work is hands-on physical repair — disassembling engines, replacing parts, hand calibration, and onsite diagnostics — which AI cannot perform without robotics that are not economically viable for this fragmented, varied work. AI might assist peripherally with diagnostic software or parts lookup, but the manual troubleshooting and repair remain firmly human. Demand is structurally tied to the installed base of motorcycles, boats, and outdoor equipment and is not heavily suppressed by cost or speed, so productivity gains would not dramatically expand the market. With disruption well below 6, this occupation is clearly resilient regardless of elasticity.

title: Social and community service managers
rationale: Disruption is moderate: many tasks like data analysis, grant proposal writing, program evaluation reporting, and outreach planning are language- and data-based and can be meaningfully accelerated by AI, but the core of the role—supervising staff, building stakeholder relationships, public speaking, community presence, and human-centered management—requires in-person judgment and trust that AI cannot replace. Elasticity is low-to-moderate because demand for social services is driven by population needs (aging adults, addiction treatment) and constrained by public and nonprofit funding budgets rather than the cost of management labor, so cheaper administration won't dramatically expand headcount. Because disruption is at or below 6, the occupation is resilient: AI augments the administrative and analytical periphery while the managerial and interpersonal core endures, with modest continued employment growth.

title: Social and human service assistants
rationale: The disruption score is moderate because while administrative tasks—researching benefits, completing paperwork, coordinating services, and documenting cases—are language-based and squarely in AI's path, the core of the work involves in-person client contact, building trust with vulnerable populations, assessing needs through human empathy, and physically traveling to clients in homes and shelters. Elasticity is moderate because demand for social services is partly suppressed by cost and staffing shortages, so cheaper coordination could unlock more service delivery, but growth is structurally capped by government funding, the population needing services, and the irreducibly human relational component. Since disruption stays at or below 6, the occupation is resilient: AI streamlines the paperwork and resource-matching periphery but the compassionate, presence-based core remains human-dependent, consistent with the projected 6% employment growth.

title: Social workers
rationale: Social work involves substantial documentation, case research, resource referrals, and report writing that AI can meaningfully assist, but the core work—building trust, assessing complex human situations, crisis intervention, advocacy, and providing emotional support and therapy—requires human empathy, presence, and judgment that AI cannot replace. The disruption score sits at moderate because AI streamlines administrative burdens (caseload paperwork, documentation) and may support clinical assessment, but face-to-face human connection remains central. Elasticity is moderate since unmet mental health and substance abuse needs are large and currently constrained, so productivity gains in administrative tasks could free workers to serve more clients, though budget constraints and licensing cap expansion. With disruption at or below 6, the occupation is resilient: AI touches the periphery (paperwork, resource matching) but does not reshape the relational and judgment-based core.

title: Sociologists
rationale: Sociologists' core work — designing research, analyzing survey/interview data, statistical analysis, and writing reports — is predominantly cognitive and language-based, putting it squarely in AI's path; AI already excels at data analysis, literature synthesis, and report drafting, though qualitative fieldwork and interviews retain some human element. Demand is constrained and largely funded by academic, government, and grant budgets that do not expand simply because research becomes cheaper, so productivity gains are unlikely to unlock proportionally more demand. With a tiny base of 3,400 jobs and inelastic, budget-capped demand, AI-driven productivity is more likely to reduce needed headcount than expand the field. High disruption combined with low elasticity places this in the replace category.

title: Software developers, quality assurance analysts, and testers
rationale: Disruption is very high because coding, testing, documentation, and design are entirely digital cognitive tasks already in the direct path of AI coding assistants and agents that materially change how developers work today. Elasticity is high because software demand is heavily suppressed by the cost and time of building it; cheaper, faster development unlocks vast latent demand as more products, integrations, security tools, and custom software get built across every industry. Because demand expansion is likely to absorb productivity gains and even grow headcount (BLS projects 15% growth), this fits augment rather than replace—though the skill set shifts toward AI-orchestration, architecture, and review.

title: Solar photovoltaic installers
rationale: The core work is overwhelmingly physical—climbing roofs, measuring, cutting, mounting panels, and wiring connections—all requiring unpredictable real-world presence and manual dexterity that AI cannot perform, so disruption is low; AI may assist only peripherally with system design, layout optimization, or scheduling. Demand elasticity is high because solar adoption is heavily cost-sensitive and currently suppressed by installation expense, so cheaper/faster processes unlock substantial latent residential and commercial demand, reflected in the projected 42% job growth. Because disruption sits at the low end (<= 6) regardless of strong demand expansion, the occupation is clearly resilient: AI touches only the planning periphery while the hands-on installation core remains human.

title: Special education teachers
rationale: Special education teaching is fundamentally an interpersonal, in-person occupation centered on patience, behavioral management, physical assistance, and emotional support for students with disabilities—tasks AI cannot perform. AI can meaningfully help with the cognitive/administrative periphery (drafting and updating IEPs, tracking progress, generating adapted lesson materials, providing assistive communication tech), but the core teaching, mentoring, and relationship-building require sustained human presence. Demand is largely fixed by school enrollments, federally mandated services, and funding constraints rather than cost or speed, so productivity gains in paperwork won't dramatically expand headcount. With disruption at the periphery only, this occupation is resilient—AI augments documentation but does not reshape the core work.

title: Special effects artists and animators
rationale: The work is almost entirely digital and creative — modeling, animation, VFX, and image generation are squarely in the path of generative AI tools that can already produce images, video, and 3D assets. Demand elasticity is high because visual content production is heavily cost- and time-constrained; cheaper production unlocks far more games, films, mobile apps, ads, and personalized media as creators and small studios who couldn't previously afford polished VFX enter the market. Because disruption is high (8) and latent demand for visual content is large and price-sensitive (7), productivity gains are likely absorbed by expanded output rather than pure headcount cuts, though individual roles will shift toward AI-directed and supervisory creative work.

title: Speech-language pathologists
rationale: Core work involves hands-on assessment, hands-on therapy for speech/swallowing muscles, and compassionate face-to-face interaction with clients and families who are often children, stroke patients, or those with autism — these require human presence and cannot be automated. AI assists with documentation, diagnostic tool selection, progress tracking, and AAC technology, but the therapeutic core remains physically and interpersonally grounded, putting disruption in the moderate range. Demand elasticity is high because speech therapy is currently underserved (long waitlists in schools, aging population, growing autism awareness), so cheaper administrative overhead could unlock more treatment, but this doesn't change the headcount picture much. With disruption at or below 6, this occupation is resilient — AI touches the periphery (notes, scheduling, assessment tools) but does not reshape the hands-on clinical core.

title: Stationary engineers and boiler operators
rationale: The core work is overwhelmingly physical and hands-on: operating, inspecting, repairing, and maintaining boilers and mechanical equipment on-site, crawling inside equipment, replacing valves and gaskets, and responding to real-time physical conditions. AI and computerized controls already assist with monitoring gauges and data logging, but the essential troubleshooting, manual repair, and licensed safety-critical presence cannot be automated. Demand is fixed by the number of physical buildings and industrial facilities requiring utilities, so cheaper monitoring software does not generate more boilers to tend. Because disruption is low and centered on peripheral monitoring tasks, the occupation is resilient regardless of elasticity.

title: Substance abuse, behavioral disorder, and mental health counselors
rationale: The core work depends on human empathy, trust-building, crisis intervention, and in-person therapeutic relationships that AI cannot replicate, though AI can assist with documentation, treatment plan drafting, screening, and triage—placing disruption at a moderate level. Demand is heavily suppressed by cost, stigma, and provider shortages, so cheaper access could unlock significant latent demand for mental health and addiction services, giving high elasticity. Despite the favorable elasticity, the disruption score remains at or below 6 because the human-centered, physically-present core tasks are largely insulated from AI, making 'resilient' the appropriate category.

title: Surgical assistants and technologists
rationale: Disruption is very low because the core work is intensely physical and hands-on—sterilizing equipment, positioning patients, passing instruments, holding retractors, suturing, and maintaining a sterile field in real-time within an operating room. These tasks require manual dexterity, physical presence, and split-second responsiveness that AI cannot replicate; AI might assist peripherally with inventory tracking or robotic surgical equipment setup but does not touch the central duties. Elasticity is moderate because surgical demand is genuinely expanding with an aging population and the shift to outpatient surgery centers, so cheaper/faster adjacent processes could unlock more procedures. Because disruption is well below the threshold, the occupation is resilient—AI affects only the edges of this physically grounded role.

title: Survey researchers
rationale: Survey research is overwhelmingly digital and cognitive work—designing questionnaires, sampling, statistical analysis, and report writing—all squarely in AI's path, with LLMs and automated analytics tools already capable of generating survey instruments, cleaning data, and producing summaries. Demand is structurally constrained and already shrinking: the BLS projects a 5% decline as data mining, big-data methods, and social media scraping displace traditional survey collection, so cheaper/faster survey work does not unlock proportional new demand. The number of distinct surveys an organization needs is relatively fixed, and alternative data sources substitute for surveys entirely, capping any expansion. High disruption combined with low, declining elasticity points to headcount contraction, fitting the replace category.

title: Surveying and mapping technicians
rationale: The work is split between physical fieldwork (visiting sites, placing markers, operating instruments, working in rugged terrain) and digital data processing (GIS, CAD, map editing, calculations). AI and automation (drones, automated data processing) materially affect the office/data portions, but the core field presence and judgment-based verification remain human-dependent, keeping disruption moderate. Demand could expand somewhat as cheaper mapping unlocks more projects, but it is structurally tied to physical construction, infrastructure, and land development activity. Since disruption is at or below 6, the occupation is classified resilient—AI reshapes the periphery and improves efficiency without eliminating the irreplaceable field-based core.

title: Surveyors
rationale: Surveying combines significant physical fieldwork (traveling to sites, taking measurements in rugged terrain, marking property lines) with cognitive office tasks like data interpretation, GIS/CAD mapping, and legal record analysis. AI, drones, and automated total stations meaningfully boost the office/analysis and data-processing portions and are already increasing productivity, but the core requires licensed human presence in the field and legally binding certification, capping disruption at moderate. Demand is somewhat tied to construction, infrastructure, and resource extraction cycles and would expand modestly if cheaper, but is structurally constrained by regulation, licensing requirements, and the fixed amount of land/projects needing surveys. Because disruption stays at or below 6, the occupation is resilient: AI reshapes the periphery and improves productivity without replacing the licensed, physically-present core work.

title: Tax examiners and collectors, and revenue agents
rationale: The core work—reviewing tax returns, verifying deductions, evaluating financial documents, matching records, and flagging discrepancies—is almost entirely digital, rule-based cognitive work directly in AI's path, with automated matching and anomaly detection already widely deployed in tax administration. Demand is highly inelastic because the volume of tax returns and collections is fixed by the number of taxpayers and statutory requirements, not by cost or speed; cheaper processing simply means fewer humans are needed rather than more auditing being demanded. Government budget constraints and the inherently capped workload reinforce headcount contraction, consistent with the BLS-projected decline. High disruption plus very low elasticity squarely fits the replace category.

title: Taxi drivers, shuttle drivers, and chauffeurs
rationale: The core work is physically driving passengers in unpredictable real-world conditions, which AI can only partially address through navigation aids and dispatch optimization today; autonomous vehicles are an emerging long-term threat but face regulatory, technical, and geographic limits that keep disruption moderate over the next decade. Demand has some elasticity—cheaper rides via automation could expand usage, and aging populations and paratransit needs add structural growth—but social, regulatory, and capital constraints cap rapid expansion. Because disruption remains at or below 6 (the physical driving task is not yet reshaped at its core within the 10-year window), the occupation is classified as resilient, with BLS even projecting above-average headcount growth.

title: Teacher assistants
rationale: The core work of teacher assistants is physical and interpersonal—supervising students, providing one-on-one attention, assisting special-needs students with feeding and hygiene, monitoring recess and buses, and managing classroom behavior. AI may help with peripheral tasks like recordkeeping, attendance, and generating learning materials, but the in-person supervision and physical caregiving cannot be automated. Demand is structurally constrained by school budgets, student-to-staff ratios, and the inherent need for human presence rather than by cost or speed of producing output, so productivity gains do not unlock large new demand. Because disruption is low and the work depends on irreplaceable physical and relational presence, this occupation is resilient to AI.

title: Technical writers
rationale: Technical writing is almost entirely language-based digital work—drafting manuals, editing, standardizing content, generating FAQs—all squarely in the direct path of LLMs that already produce competent documentation from product specs. Demand elasticity is low because documentation needs are largely fixed by the number of products and features shipped; cheaper writing does not cause companies to produce dramatically more manuals, though some latent demand for richer, multi-format content exists. With disruption at 8 and elasticity at 4, productivity gains translate mostly into fewer writers needed per project rather than expanded output, consistent with BLS noting AI will suppress already-flat employment growth.

title: Telecommunications technicians
rationale: Disruption is low because the core work is physical: climbing towers, splicing fiber optic cables, installing equipment in homes, digging trenches, and working in cramped or elevated spaces. AI can assist with remote diagnostics, network monitoring, and troubleshooting (central office technicians already correct issues remotely), but the hands-on installation and repair tasks require unpredictable real-world presence and dexterity that AI cannot replace. Elasticity is low-to-moderate because demand is driven by infrastructure buildout cycles (5G, broadband expansion) that are largely complete, and newer fiber technologies require less frequent maintenance—productivity gains don't unlock much new physical demand. Since disruption is well under 6, this occupation is resilient: AI touches the monitoring and diagnostic periphery but leaves the physical core intact.

title: Tellers
rationale: Teller work is a mix of physical cash handling and digital transaction processing; while ATMs, mobile banking, and enhanced kiosks already automate much of the routine work, the in-person presence, identity verification, and customer-service interaction keep a human element, putting disruption at a moderate level rather than fully digital. Demand is highly inelastic—people do not perform dramatically more banking transactions just because they are cheaper or faster; the volume is structurally fixed and already shifting away from branches. Despite low elasticity, the disruption score falls at 6 (driven mainly by automation eliminating positions rather than AI reshaping the core human-facing role), so it lands in the resilient category by the threshold rule, though the occupation is clearly contracting due to broader automation and branch closures rather than generative AI specifically.

title: Top executives
rationale: Top executive work involves substantial cognitive tasks like analyzing financial reports, identifying cost savings, and formulating strategy that AI tools can meaningfully augment, but the core of the job—leadership, accountability, negotiation, high-stakes judgment, stakeholder relationships, and bearing ultimate responsibility for organizational outcomes—is inherently human and not in AI's direct path. AI will reshape how executives gather information and model decisions but cannot assume the legal, fiduciary, and social authority the role requires. Demand for executives is structurally fixed by the number of organizations rather than the cost or speed of executive output, so productivity gains do not unlock proportionally more demand. With disruption at or below 6, the occupation is resilient: AI touches the analytical periphery while the decision-making and leadership core remains intact.

title: Tour and travel guides
rationale: The core work is physical, in-person, and interpersonal — escorting groups, reading the room, adapting to weather and group needs, and providing live entertainment and human rapport. AI can assist with peripheral tasks like research, route planning, itinerary logistics, and language translation, but it cannot replace the embodied presence and personal engagement that define the role. Demand for guided experiences could expand somewhat as travel and leisure grow and AI lowers planning costs, but it's tied to physical tourism volume rather than unleashed by cheap digital output. With disruption well below 6, this occupation is resilient regardless of elasticity.

title: Training and development managers
rationale: The role involves substantial knowledge work—designing training content, selecting materials, evaluating program effectiveness—much of which AI tools (content generation, personalized learning platforms, analytics) can directly accelerate, pushing disruption toward the high end. However, core managerial duties like aligning training with business strategy, supervising staff, budgeting, and stakeholder collaboration require human judgment and presence, keeping disruption at a moderate 6. Demand is moderately elastic: cheaper, AI-personalized training could expand reskilling efforts as workforces face continuous change, but headcount of managers (versus content output) is structurally capped. Since disruption is 6 (<=6), the occupation falls into resilient—AI reshapes how content and delivery work but the managerial core remains intact.

title: Training and development specialists
rationale: Disruption is high because core tasks—designing training materials, creating online learning modules, developing course content, and assessing needs through surveys—are largely digital and language-based, areas where generative AI already excels at content creation, instructional design, and personalization. However, the in-person delivery, facilitation, and interpersonal collaboration portions retain a human element, keeping it from the very-high tier. Elasticity is high because cheaper, faster training content production unlocks substantial latent demand: continuous upskilling driven by rapid technological change, regulatory compliance training, and personalized learning that was previously too costly to develop at scale. With AI dramatically lowering content production costs, organizations will produce far more tailored training, expanding total demand enough to absorb productivity gains and supporting the BLS-projected 11% growth.

title: Transportation, storage, and distribution managers
rationale: Disruption is moderate because while AI strongly enhances the analytical and planning portions of the job—route optimization, demand forecasting, inventory tracking, and supply chain coordination—the core role centers on supervising staff, physical facility oversight, resolving real-time disruptions, and leadership functions that require human presence and judgment. Elasticity is moderate as cheaper, faster logistics analysis enables more sophisticated supply chain operations and e-commerce growth, but headcount is tied to the physical footprint of warehouses, fleets, and facilities that must be managed regardless of AI efficiency gains. Because disruption stays at or below 6, the occupation is resilient: AI reshapes the data-driven planning tools these managers use but does not displace the supervisory, interpersonal, and on-site problem-solving that defines the role.

title: Travel agents
rationale: The core work — searching fares, building itineraries, comparing options, booking reservations, and advising on documents — is almost entirely digital, language-based, and information-retrieval work that AI and online booking platforms already perform directly; this has been eroding the occupation for two decades and AI accelerates it further. Demand elasticity is low because total travel volume is constrained by household budgets and time, not by the cost of booking; cheaper agent services do not dramatically increase how many trips people take, and self-service tools already absorb much of the latent demand. With disruption very high and elasticity weak, productivity gains translate into fewer agents rather than expanded output, fitting the replace category, though a residual niche for complex, high-touch, or luxury planning persists.

title: Tutors
rationale: Tutoring is predominantly cognitive, language-based instruction that AI can directly perform—explaining concepts, generating practice problems, providing feedback, and adapting to student level are all squarely in AI's path, driving a high disruption score. However, demand for personalized education is heavily suppressed by cost and access, so dramatically cheaper, scalable AI-assisted tutoring unlocks enormous latent demand across underserved students and subjects. While pure commodity homework-help may shift to software, human tutors who leverage AI for personalized, high-touch, motivational, and special-needs instruction can serve far more students, keeping headcount stable or growing. The combination of high disruption and high elasticity fits the augment category, even though BLS projects flat near-term growth.

title: Umpires, referees, and other sports officials
rationale: The core work is physical and presence-based: positioning oneself on the field, making split-second visual judgments, running/squatting for extended periods, and managing human disputes with coaches and players. AI-assisted technologies (video replay, automated ball-strike systems, goal-line tech) augment certain calls but do not replace the human official who manages the game, enforces rules, and provides the social authority that participants accept. Demand is tied to the number of games played, which expands with growing sports participation but is structurally bounded by the number of contests rather than by cost of officiating. Because disruption stays low and the work remains fundamentally physical and in-person, the occupation is resilient.

title: Urban and regional planners
rationale: Much of planning involves cognitive, data-driven work — GIS analysis, data gathering, feasibility assessment, and report writing — which AI tools can materially accelerate, pushing disruption to the moderate-high boundary. However, the core work also involves stakeholder negotiation, public meetings, political judgment, site inspection, and discretionary decisions on plan approval that require human presence and accountability, capping disruption at 6.
